topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Comparing groups: more or fewer
topic.description: Compare two groups of objects to determine which has more, fewer, or whether they are equal, using matching and counting strategies
evidence: Use one-to-one matching to compare two groups
State which group has more/fewer after counting both
Use the language 'equal to', 'more than', 'less than', 'fewer', 'most', 'least'
topic.assessmentPrompt: If you put 6 raisins in one hand and 4 in the other and ask {{name}} which hand has more, can they work it out — either by counting or just by looking?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Ages 4–6 (Reception/Kindergarten → Year 1). COMPARING TWO GROUPS — deciding which has more, fewer, or whether they are equal, using one-to-one MATCHING and/or counting. Builds the relational meaning of number and the vocabulary that later attaches to <, >, =.
• Standards — UK (DfE): NC Year 1 'use the language of: equal to, more than, less than (fewer), most, least'; identify and represent/compare numbers with objects. Year 2 formalises comparison with the <, >, = signs to 100. EYFS 'Numerical Patterns' (compare quantities to 10).
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): K.CC.6 verbatim — 'Identify whether the number of objects in one group is greater than, less than, or equal to the number of objects in another group, e.g., by using matching and counting strategies' (groups of up to ten). K.CC.7 then compares written numerals 1–10.
• Operational details: Teach TWO strategies — (1) MATCHING (pair objects one-to-one; a leftover = more, none left over = equal) and (2) COUNTING both and comparing the counts. Matching works before secure counting and directly confronts the length/spacing illusion. Stage the Piagetian conservation trap: a spread-out row of 5 vs a bunched row of 6 — 'longer' ≠ 'more'. Nail the vocabulary, especially 'fewer' (countable groups) and 'equal to'.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (4–5) matches two small groups one-to-one and says which has more/fewer or if equal. Tier B (5–6) compares groups to 10 by counting both, using 'more than / fewer than / equal to' correctly. Tier C (6) is not fooled when the larger group is bunched shorter than a spread-out smaller group; justifies by matching or counting.
bestPractices: Teach MATCHING first: line up and pair the two groups; the unmatched leftover shows 'more', a clean pairing shows 'equal' — a strategy that works before counting is secure.
Then connect to COUNTING: count both, the larger count = more; show the two strategies agree.
Deliberately confront conservation: compare a spread-out 5 with a bunched 6 so 'longer row' is caught out; demand a matching/counting justification, not a glance.
Drill precise language — 'fewer' vs 'less', 'equal to'; model full sentences ('7 is more than 5').
Show equal and unequal groups side by side and ask 'how could we make them equal?' (add or remove one — links to one-more/one-less).
keyRepresentations: Two rows lined up for one-to-one matching (connect-the-pairs; the leftover).
Two ten-frames side by side (empty cells show the gap).
Cube towers stood next to each other (taller = more; same height = equal).
A balance / see-saw image for 'equal to'.
commonMisconceptions: Length/spacing = number: judging the longer or more spread-out row as 'more' regardless of count (the classic conservation error).
Using 'bigger' / 'taller' loosely instead of comparing quantity; confusing 'fewer' with 'smaller objects'.
Comparing by which row 'ends further along' rather than by matching or counting.
Believing two groups can't be equal if the objects look different or are arranged differently.

learn.summary: For ages 4–6, teach children to compare two groups and decide which has more, fewer, or whether they are equal, using one-to-one matching and counting. The central challenge is the conservation-of-number trap: a longer or more spread-out row can look like 'more' even when it has fewer items. Matching one-to-one (and counting both groups) resolves the comparison and builds the vocabulary — 'more than', 'fewer than', 'equal to' — that later attaches to <, >, =.

activities.title: Match the two rows and find the leftover
feedback: If every object is paired and none is left over, the two groups are equal.
If one row has an object with no partner, that row has more and the other has fewer.
If you want to make the groups equal, add one object at a time to the smaller group or take one at a time away from the larger, checking the pairing again each time, until no object is left over.
When every object is identical (same-size cubes, same-weight objects), cube towers and a level balance are other ways to show 'equal': same height, or the see-saw sitting level.
activities.rationale: Matching one-to-one gives a direct, concrete meaning of more/fewer/equal that does not depend on secure counting, and sets up the comparison language. An interactive pairing (drag-to-pair or tap-to-match, with the leftover highlighted and a 'make it fair' add/remove control), towers of identical cubes, or a balance image with identical same-weight objects each make the relationship visible; keep groups to ten per K.CC.6.
sourceClaims: K.CC.6: 'Identify whether the number of objects in one group is greater than, less than, or equal to the number of objects in another group, e.g., by using matching and counting strategies' (up to ten objects).
Year 1: 'use the language of: equal to, more than, less than (fewer), most, least'; Year 2 introduces the <, >, = signs and compares/orders numbers 0–100.
learnerActions: Set up two rows of objects and pair each object in the top row with one in the bottom row (draw a connecting line, or drag a string from each to its partner).
When one or more objects are left with no partner, say that row has MORE (and the other row has FEWER); when every object is paired, say the rows are EQUAL.

As an alternative, build the two groups as towers of identical cubes stood side by side (taller tower = more, same height = equal), or, using only identical objects of the same weight, use a balance/see-saw image to show two equal groups level each other.
Read off a full sentence about the two groups you built, using the frame '__ is more than __' or '__ is equal to __' with your own counts.
Use a 'make it fair' action: add or take away one object until every object pairs up and both rows read EQUAL.
activities.intendedInsight: Pairing objects one-to-one shows which group has more (a leftover) or whether they are equal (a clean pairing) — a strategy that works even before counting is secure.

activities.title: Count both groups and compare
feedback: If both strategies point to the same group (or both show the groups are equal), you can be confident in your comparison.
Remember 'fewer' is about how many items there are, not how big the items are — use identical objects and compare the counts.
If you count correctly but pick the wrong comparison word, slow down on the words 'more than', 'fewer than', 'equal to' — the counting itself was fine.
activities.rationale: Counting both groups connects the relational comparison to cardinality, and showing matching and counting agree strengthens confidence. Ten-frames side by side expose the gap between counts, and using identical objects isolates number from size so 'fewer' is not confused with 'smaller'.
sourceClaims: K.CC.6: 'Identify whether the number of objects in one group is greater than, less than, or equal to the number of objects in another group, e.g., by using matching and counting strategies' (up to ten objects).
learnerActions: Count the objects in each group aloud.
Place the two groups in ten-frames side by side so the empty cells make the gap between the counts easy to see.
Compare the two counts: if one is larger, name that group as having 'more than' the other and the other as having 'fewer than'; if the counts match, say the groups are 'equal to' each other.
Check your answer against the matching method and notice the two strategies agree.
Practise the words 'fewer' and 'equal to' in full sentences, using identical objects so only the number differs.
activities.intendedInsight: Counting both groups and comparing the counts gives the same answer as matching; the larger count means more, and matching counts mean equal.

activities.title: The conservation trap: longer isn't always more
feedback: Spreading a row out makes it longer but does not add any objects — the count stays the same.
If a short bunched row of 6 beats a long spread-out row of 5, matching the strings or counting proves it: the longer look was misleading.
If you judged by length, line the two rows up one above the other, starting at the same end, and match one-to-one so the leftover object is visible, then count both aloud.
activities.rationale: Directly confronting the length/spacing illusion is the core conceptual work of this topic. Having the child commit to a prediction first and then check by matching/counting surfaces the misconception and provides the evidence to correct it. A spacing toggle that bunches or spreads a row stages this comparison concretely.
sourceClaims: Young children mis-judge which group has more by row length/spacing rather than number (conservation of number); one-to-one matching is the antidote.
learnerActions: Look at a spread-out row of 5 next to a bunched-together row of 6; before matching or counting, predict which has more and say why.
Then match the rows one-to-one (or count both) to check which actually has more — here the bunched row of 6 wins even though the spread-out row of 5 looks longer.
Take two equal rows, spread one out into a long line, and predict whether spreading changed how many there are — then check by matching or counting.
Explain in your own words why the longer-looking line does not always have more.
activities.intendedInsight: Spreading objects out or bunching them up does not change how many there are; the longer row is not necessarily the one with more.

constraints: Keep groups to no more than ten objects, consistent with K.CC.6.

A static labelled 'more/fewer/equal' picture can serve as a reference but does not let the child match, count, or rearrange to resolve a comparison; it is a reference scaffold, not a substitute for the child doing the matching.

Multiple-choice 'which has more?' items and categorising pairs into more/fewer/equal can check whether a child can pick the right comparison, but do not themselves require the child to construct the matching or justify it.
A fairness conversation ('who has more sweets — is that fair?') can frame the task and motivate the vocabulary; it does not itself settle the comparison, which is resolved by matching or counting.
Use identical objects when first teaching 'fewer' so children do not confuse 'more items' with 'bigger items'.

Expectations by stage: younger children match two small groups and say which has more/fewer or if equal; others compare groups to ten by counting both; the most secure are not fooled when the larger group is bunched shorter than a spread-out smaller group and justify by matching or counting.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources have not been re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The conservation-of-number source is marked unverified (verified:false) in the original row; the copied claim that one-to-one matching is 'the antidote' to the length/spacing illusion is presented as a teaching proposal, not an established comparative result.

The original row asserted 3D depth 'only clutters' comparison and that comparison 'is settled by matching/counting, not talk'; these categorical medium claims have been dropped or softened to scoped affordance notes rather than universal claims about what media can or cannot teach.

Example number pairs differ across the original fields (5 vs 6 in the interactive, 6 vs 7 in the assessment); either works for the conservation trap as long as the shorter-looking row genuinely has more — both kept as illustrative, not canonical.
Ten-frames, cube towers, and the balance/see-saw image are drawn from the original keyRepresentations and offered as optional alternatives, not required tools.

assess.poeTask: Lay out two rows of 6, matched one-to-one, and agree together they are the same. Ask the child to PREDICT before you act: 'If I spread THIS row out into a long line, will it have more, fewer, or the same — and why?' They commit to a reason first; then spread it and check by matching/counting. 'The same, you didn't add or take any' is conservation; 'more, it's longer now' reveals the length-for-number misconception.
probeDeeper: Show me how you could match them up to check.
If I pushed Row A's counters close together like Row B, which would have more then?
How many more does Row B have?
Can you change them so the two rows are equal?
assess.correctAnswer: Row B has more — it has 7 and Row A has 6. I matched (or counted) them; the longer-looking line isn't always the one with more.

errorPatterns.pattern: length stands in for number — judges the longer or more spread-out row as 'more' regardless of count ('this one has more, it's longer')
errorPatterns.nextMove: line the two rows up end-to-end and match one-to-one so the leftover counter is visible; count both aloud; then squeeze/spread a row to show number doesn't change with length
errorPatterns.distractor: Row A has more because it's longer.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: picks the visually longer Row A and, asked how, points to its length rather than a count

errorPatterns.pattern: 'more' taken as bigger or longer objects rather than more items
errorPatterns.nextMove: use identical objects and stress 'more' = greater number, established by matching one-to-one
errorPatterns.revealedBy: chooses the row with larger counters or the longer line even when items are identical

errorPatterns.pattern: counts both correctly but names the wrong one as 'more', or cannot yet use 'fewer'/'equal' precisely
errorPatterns.nextMove: scaffold comparison language on a number track (the later number is more); rehearse 'fewer' and 'equal' explicitly — do not reteach the counting itself
errorPatterns.revealedBy: accurate counts (6 and 7) but the comparison word is wrong or missing

responseLevels.gap: Chooses by appearance — the longer or more spread-out row 'has more' — and is not moved by matching or counting.
responseLevels.full: Determines more/fewer/equal by matching or counting even when appearance conflicts, explains the longer line isn't necessarily more, and uses the comparison language accurately.
responseLevels.partial: Counts both rows correctly but leans on the count alone; unsettled when appearance and number conflict, or cannot yet use 'fewer'/'equal' precisely.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are two rows of counters. (Set up Row A as 6 counters spread out into a long line, and Row B as 7 counters bunched close together, so Row A LOOKS longer.) Which row has more counters — or are they the same? How can you be sure?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: This pits appearance against number. A child who compares by number — matching one-to-one or counting both — finds Row B has more despite looking shorter. A child who compares by appearance picks the longer Row A ('it's more spread out'). The 'how can you be sure' tier forces the method: matching/counting versus looking-longer, which is exactly the conservation-of-number divide.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: How Many in Total?
topic.description: Cardinality principle: the last number said when counting a set tells how many objects are in the set, regardless of arrangement or order counted
evidence: After counting a set, answer 'how many?' with the last number stated
Understand that rearranging objects does not change the count
Understand that counting in a different order gives the same total
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} counts out 7 toy cars and you ask "so how many cars are there?", do they say "7" straight away — or do they count them all again from the start?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Ages 4–6 (Reception/Kindergarten → Year 1). THE CARDINALITY PRINCIPLE — the last number word said when counting a set tells HOW MANY (its numerosity), and that total is unchanged by rearrangement or the order counted. The bridge from counting-as-reciting to counting-as-quantity; prerequisite for +1, comparison, number representation and all early addition/subtraction (centrality 0.97).
• Standards — UK (DfE): EYFS 'Number' ELG (deep understanding of number to 10). NC Year 1 'count, read and write numbers to 100' and 'given a number, identify 1 more and 1 less' presuppose cardinality; the language 'equal to, more than, less than (fewer), most, least' is Year 1.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): K.CC.4b verbatim — 'Understand that the last number name said tells the number of objects counted. The number of objects is the same regardless of their arrangement or the order in which they were counted.' K.CC.4 heads this as 'connect counting to cardinality.'
• Operational details: 'How many?' and 'give me N' are the canonical assessments — a child who RECOUNTS when asked 'how many?' has not grasped it (Thompson). Confront arrangement-invariance: count, then spread out / bunch up / recount in a different order → same total. Subitising small sets (≤5) supports instant cardinality. Use the Bermejo 'start counting at three' probe to distinguish TRUE cardinality from last-word parroting.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (4–5) after counting ≤5 answers 'how many?' with the last word without recounting, and gives-N for N≤5. Tier B (5–6) knows rearranging a counted set of ≤10 doesn't change the total, without recounting. Tier C (6) sees the total is unchanged when counted from a different starting object/order and isn't fooled by spreading the set out (early conservation).
bestPractices: Emphasise the last word's DOUBLE job — it names the final object AND tells the whole set's size (Thompson); mark the shift with stress/gesture: '…four, five — FIVE altogether!'
Use 'give me N' tasks (child counts out a subset) as the strongest cardinality check — harder and less gameable than 'how many?'.
Confront arrangement-invariance directly: count, then move/scatter the same objects and ask 'how many now?'; the child who must recount reveals the gap.
Probe with the Bermejo trick — ask the child to start counting 5 objects from 'three'; answering 'seven' (last word) rather than 'five' exposes last-word parroting, not cardinality.
Build subitising (instant recognition of ≤5) with dot cards, dice and ten-frames so small quantities are known as wholes, reinforcing number = amount.
keyRepresentations: Ten-frame / five-frame (the filled frame shows the total as a stable whole).
Dot / dice / domino patterns for subitising (cardinality without counting).
The 'count → cover it → how many?' routine (forces recall of the total, not a recount).
A numeral card placed beside a counted set (numeral ↔ quantity).
commonMisconceptions: Recounting when asked 'how many?' — treating the count as a performance rather than something that yields a total (the diagnostic error).
Last-word parroting without meaning — repeating the final word said even when the count started at the wrong number (Bermejo: counts 5 from 'three', answers 'seven').
Believing rearranging or spreading out a set changes how many there are (pre-conservation; length/spacing mistaken for quantity).
Thinking the last number names only the last OBJECT, not the whole set.

learn.summary: Help children aged 4–6 grasp the cardinality principle: the last number word said when counting a set tells how many objects there are (its total), and that total does not change when the objects are rearranged or counted in a different order. This is the bridge from counting-as-reciting to counting-as-quantity and underpins +1/−1, comparison and early addition/subtraction. Useful checks include 'how many?' answered without recounting, 'give me exactly N', and arrangement/order-invariance probes.

activities.title: Count, scatter, re-ask: the total that stays put
feedback: If the child says the same number without recounting and explains 'you didn't add or take any away', affirm: that reasoning is conservation of number.
If the child insists on recounting after rearrangement, rearrange back and forth while asking each time 'did I add any or take any away?' to surface that nothing changed.

If the child says 'fewer, it's a smaller pile' or 'more, it's spread out', lay out a second matching set in the original arrangement and pair each moved object one-to-one with an object in that set, so the child can see none are left over and the quantity is the same.
Mark the shift from naming the last object to naming the whole set with stress and gesture on the total: '…four, five — FIVE altogether!'
activities.rationale: Directly confronting arrangement-invariance (count, then move the same objects and re-ask) targets the diagnostic error of recounting and the pre-conservation belief that spreading/bunching changes quantity. A persistent visible total makes the invariance concrete.
sourceClaims: Cardinal principle: the final number name tells the numerosity of the set, not just names the last object; a child who recounts when asked 'how many?' has not grasped it. Bermejo et al. (2004): asked to count five objects starting from 'three', many children answer 'seven' (the last word said) — showing last-word repetition ≠ cardinal understanding.
K.CC.4b: 'Understand that the last number name said tells the number of objects counted. The number of objects is the same regardless of their arrangement or the order in which they were counted.'
learnerActions: Count a small set of objects aloud (start with 5, e.g. five toy ducks or cars) and say the total: '…four, five — five altogether!'
Place or keep visible a total badge/numeral card showing the count beside the set.
Now move the same objects around: bunch them in a corner, spread them out in a ring or long line — without adding or removing any.

Before recounting, say how many there are now and explain why (if the total card is still showing, ask why the card still matches the set, so the answer is reasoned rather than simply read off the card).
Check by recounting together only if needed, and notice the total is the same.
activities.intendedInsight: Moving objects around cannot change how many there are; the total is a fixed property of the set, so you do not need to recount after rearranging.

activities.title: Give me exactly N (count-out task)
feedback: If the child counts past the requested number or hands over too few, gently restart and emphasise stopping at the target word.
If the child cannot stop at the requested amount, return to 'count then say the total' tasks before retrying count-out.

Count-out is harder and less gameable than 'how many?'; consistent success across several requests, including larger numbers such as 5 or more, is strong evidence of cardinality rather than of last-word repetition.
activities.rationale: 'Give me N' tasks require the child to use the number word as a target quantity, which recognition or last-word repetition cannot easily fake (though a correct answer with a very small N can come from knowing small numbers rather than general cardinality), so they complement the 'how many?' check. (The supporting source establishes the cardinality principle these tasks draw on, not the method's measured effectiveness.)
sourceClaims: Cardinal principle: the final number name tells the numerosity of the set, not just names the last object; a child who recounts when asked 'how many?' has not grasped it. Bermejo et al. (2004): asked to count five objects starting from 'three', many children answer 'seven' (the last word said) — showing last-word repetition ≠ cardinal understanding.
learnerActions: From a heap or big box of objects, count out exactly a requested number (e.g. 'give me exactly 5 cars', 'give me exactly 4').
Stop as soon as the requested amount is reached, rather than counting the whole heap.
Check the handed-over set by recounting together.
activities.intendedInsight: A number word is a stop-signal for a specific quantity: knowing 'five' means being able to produce a set of exactly five, not just reciting up to five.

activities.title: Start counting from three (parroting trap)
feedback: If the child answers 'seven', recount normally from one together and compare: the set had five objects both times.
If the child answers 'five', acknowledge they are tracking the actual quantity, not the last word spoken.
Use this as a diagnostic probe, not a correction exercise — the goal is to focus attention on what the final number means.
activities.rationale: The Bermejo 'start at three' probe distinguishes true cardinality from last-word parroting, which a simple 'how many?' after a normal count may not expose.
sourceClaims: Cardinal principle: the final number name tells the numerosity of the set, not just names the last object; a child who recounts when asked 'how many?' has not grasped it. Bermejo et al. (2004): asked to count five objects starting from 'three', many children answer 'seven' (the last word said) — showing last-word repetition ≠ cardinal understanding.
learnerActions: Lay out 5 objects. The adult asks the child to count them but to START saying 'three' on the first object, then 'four', 'five', 'six', 'seven'.
Afterwards ask: 'So how many objects are there really?'
Discuss why the answer is still five even though the last word said was 'seven'.
activities.intendedInsight: The correct total (five) is a property of the set, not just whatever word you happen to say last; answering 'seven' may mean the child is repeating the last word rather than finding how many (or may reflect confusion about the unusual instruction).

activities.title: Count from the other end (order-irrelevance)
feedback: If the child predicts a different number for a different starting point, do NOT mark it wrong — let them count both ways carefully (touching each object once) and discover the totals match; if they get different totals, recount slowly together to find the skipped or double-counted object.
Genuine order-irrelevance develops late, so build it through repeated hands-on experience rather than correction.
activities.rationale: Order-irrelevance develops late and is built through repeated experience, so letting the child count both ways and discover that the totals match is preferable to correcting a prediction; premature marking-wrong does not accelerate the understanding.
sourceClaims: K.CC.4b: 'Understand that the last number name said tells the number of objects counted. The number of objects is the same regardless of their arrangement or the order in which they were counted.'
learnerActions: Count a line of objects left-to-right and say the total.
Count the same line right-to-left (or starting from a middle object) and say the total again.
Compare: as long as each object is counted exactly once, the total is the same whichever object you start from and whatever order you count in.
activities.intendedInsight: The total does not depend on which object you count first or the order you count in.

activities.title: Subitising small sets as wholes
feedback: If the child counts one-by-one on a quick flash, shorten the exposure and start with 2 or 3 before building to 5.
After covering the set, if the child wants to uncover and recount, prompt 'you already counted — how many were there?' to encourage recall of the total.
activities.rationale: Subitising and the cover-and-recall routine may support cardinality by presenting small sets as stable wholes and prompting recall of a total rather than a recount. The supporting source frames subitising as part of a developmental progression toward number sense, but that source is unverified, so this is a qualified proposal.
sourceClaims: Subitising and comparing magnitudes support number sense in early years as part of a developmental progression toward cardinality.
learnerActions: Briefly show dot cards, dice faces, domino patterns or a five-frame (or a ten-frame filled only partly) showing small quantities (≤5) and say how many without counting one-by-one.
Match a numeral card to a set to link the symbol to the quantity.
Use the 'count → cover it → how many?' routine: count a set, cover it, then recall the total from memory instead of recounting.
activities.intendedInsight: Small quantities can be recognised instantly as whole amounts, reinforcing that a number names an amount, and the total can be recalled rather than re-derived.

activities.title: Predict-then-check: will bunching change how many? (assessment companion)
feedback: 'The same, because you didn't add or take any away' is the target conservation reasoning — affirm it.
'Fewer, it's a smaller pile' or 'more, it's spread out' signals number is not yet conserved; rearrange back and forth asking 'did I add or take any away?' and use one-to-one matching.

'You'd have to count them again to know' signals the child does not yet trust that rearranging leaves the total unchanged; rearrange back and forth asking 'did I add or take any away?', and add count-out tasks and the cover-and-recall routine.
activities.rationale: Asking the child to commit to a prediction and a reason BEFORE observing makes the diagnostic distinction between conservation reasoning and appearance-based judgement explicit.
sourceClaims: K.CC.4b: 'Understand that the last number name said tells the number of objects counted. The number of objects is the same regardless of their arrangement or the order in which they were counted.'
learnerActions: Show 5 cars in a line and agree there are 5.
Before anything is moved, PREDICT: 'If I bunch these into a pile, will there be more, fewer, or the same — and why?' Commit to a reason first.
Then bunch them and count together to check against the prediction.
Afterwards answer: 'How could you have known it would still be 5 without counting?'
activities.intendedInsight: The reason given before observing reveals understanding: 'the same, because you didn't add or take any' shows conservation; 'fewer, it's a smaller pile' does not.

constraints: Target standards: EYFS 'Number' ELG (deep understanding of number to 10); CCSS-M K.CC.4b and K.CC.4 ('connect counting to cardinality'); NC Year 1 '1 more/1 less' and the language 'equal to, more than, less than (fewer), most, least' presuppose cardinality.
A child who RECOUNTS when asked 'how many?' after a completed count may not yet have grasped cardinality — this is a key diagnostic sign, best confirmed with give-N and other probes.

Progression checkpoints: Tier A (4–5) answers 'how many?' with the last word without recounting and gives-N for N≤5; Tier B (5–6) knows rearranging a counted set of ≤10 does not change the total without recounting; Tier C (6) sees the total is unchanged when counted from a different start/order and is not fooled by spreading out (early conservation).
Order-irrelevance and conservation develop late; build them through experience and do not mark a child wrong for predicting a different total before they have discovered otherwise.

A static labelled scene ('5 counted, 5 altogether') can serve as a reference but cannot by itself animate the rearrange-and-recheck that demonstrates invariance; use it alongside hands-on rearrangement.

Multiple-choice or slider-style response formats ('how many altogether?', 'same or different total?', give-N via slider) can serve as an assessment companion; recognition-only responses do not themselves elicit the independent count-out production that most strongly evidences cardinality.
A screen 'persistent total badge' or live recolouring/dragging is one optional way to make invariance visible; physical objects a child can move by hand serve the same purpose and are equally valid.
Keep sets small to preserve focus on the small-set quantity; avoid cluttered or busy displays that distract from the quantity itself.

A last-word parroter recounts the pile or gives a new number — for them '5' was an echo of the last word, not the set's total. A child lacking conservation says there are now more/fewer because the pile 'looks different'. The 'without counting again... how do you know' tier separates knowing the total from re-deriving it.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Ages 4–6 (Reception/Kindergarten → Year 1). THE SUCCESSOR PRINCIPLE — each successive counting number represents a quantity ONE LARGER than the previous (and one less going back). Turns the flat count sequence into a structure of +1 steps; the seed of the number line, counting-on and early addition/subtraction.
• Standards — UK (DfE): NC Year 1 'given a number, identify 1 more and 1 less'; represent numbers on the number line (Y1). EYFS 'Numerical Patterns' (one more / one less within 10). Extends to 10-more/10-less (Y2–Y3).
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): K.CC.4c verbatim — 'Understand that each successive number name refers to a quantity that is one larger.'
• Operational details: Link the spoken sequence to quantity change — add exactly ONE object and the count moves to the next word; on a number line/track +1 is a step right, −1 a step left. Teach 'one more' and 'one less' TOGETHER as inverse moves. Counting-on (from 5, 'one more' = 6 without restarting at 1) is the payoff and depends on cardinality. Use a staircase/tower image (each step one cube taller).
• Checkpoint: Tier A (4–5) given ≤5 objects, knows adding one makes the next number ('one more than 4 is 5'). Tier B (5–6) gives one more AND one less for numbers to 10 without recounting from 1. Tier C (6) explains one step along the number line is +1 and links it to counting-on for addition.
bestPractices: Pair the word-step with a quantity-step: add exactly one object as you say the next number, so 'the next number' MEANS 'one more thing'.
Teach one-more and one-less as inverse moves on the same model (number track hops right/left), not as two unrelated facts.
Make counting-on explicit: from a known total, say the next number WITHOUT restarting at one — this requires cardinality and bridges to addition.
Use a staircase / number track so +1 is a single visible step; contrast with a two-step jump (foreshadows skip counting).
Ask prediction questions ('if we add one more cube, what number?') before acting, then check — builds the expectation that each step is exactly one.
keyRepresentations: Number track / number line (steps of one; right = more, left = less).
Cube tower / staircase (each step one taller).
Ten-frame filled one cell at a time.
'One more / one less' arrow cards or a +1/−1 machine.
commonMisconceptions: Recounting from 1 to find 'one more' instead of counting-on (successor not yet linked to cardinality).
Knowing 'one more' but not 'one less' — the backward direction lags because the string is learned forward only.
Treating 'one more' as merely 'the next word I say' rather than a quantity one larger (fails when the count starts wrong).
Not realising every step is exactly one — thinking numbers grow by an inconsistent amount.

learn.summary: For ages 4–6 (Reception/Kindergarten to Year 1): the successor principle — each successive counting number names a quantity exactly ONE larger than the one before, and going back one is one less. The aim is to turn the flat count sequence into a structure of +1 / −1 steps, laying the ground for the number line, counting-on and early addition/subtraction. Teach 'one more' and 'one less' together as inverse moves, link the spoken word-step to an actual quantity-step, and build towards counting-on (finding 'one more than 5' as 6 without restarting at 1).

activities.title: One more, one less in lockstep
feedback: If a learner adds one cube but names a number that skips ahead (e.g. says '10' after 6), pause and count the cubes together: adding one object moves the count to the very next word only.

If a learner can give 'one more' easily but stalls on 'one less', treat the backward direction as its own game on the same track rather than as a failure — counting back develops separately and matures with practice.
When a prediction matches the result, name the structure out loud: 'Each step added exactly one, so the number went up by one.'
If the learner struggles with a decade boundary such as 'one more than 9', slow down and step the marker one place so they see 9 then 10 is a single step.
activities.rationale: Pairing the spoken word-step with an added object makes 'the next number' mean 'one more thing', and enacting both directions on one shared model presents one-more and one-less as inverse moves rather than two unrelated facts. Prediction-then-check builds the expectation that each step is exactly one.
sourceClaims: K.CC.4c: 'Understand that each successive number name refers to a quantity that is one larger.'
Year 1: 'given a number, identify 1 more and 1 less'; identify and represent numbers using the number line.
Counting-on and the number line as steps of one are foundational representations bridging counting to addition/subtraction (concrete–pictorial–abstract).
learnerActions: Build a tower with cubes (or fill a ten-frame one cell at a time) and say the count as you go.
Before adding, predict: 'If I add one more cube, what number will it be?' Then add exactly one cube and check that the count moves to the next word.
Add one cube and say the next number in the same beat, so that 'the next number' means 'one more thing'.
Now remove one cube and say the number that is one less, naming it as the mirror move of adding one.
On a number track, hop a marker (or a frog along lily-pads) exactly one place right for 'one more' and one place left for 'one less'.
activities.intendedInsight: Each successive counting number is a quantity exactly one larger than the previous one, and one back is exactly one smaller; +1 and −1 are a single step in opposite directions on the same track.

activities.title: Counting on from a hidden total
feedback: Correct answer to 7 + 1 is 8, because one more than 7 is the next counting number; adding one moves you one step up the count.

If the learner must open the box and recount from 1, do not force counting-on before it emerges: play 'one more' with a covered set and a number track so they repeatedly see 7→8 as a single step. It matures with practice.
If the learner names a non-successor such as 'ten' or 'lots', reteach with a visible add-one-and-count on a number track, showing 7 then 8 is exactly one step, and anchor 'one more = next number'.
activities.rationale: Hiding the set discourages recounting, so answering without opening the box calls for linking the count sequence to +1 — the heart of counting-on and the bridge from counting to addition. It can also help reveal which learners currently use the successor idea and which still rely on counting from one, though one observation is not a definitive judgement.

learnerActions: Count a set of objects into a box or under a cover, then agree on how many are inside (e.g. 7).
With the set hidden, drop in exactly one more and answer, without recounting, how many there are now.
Explain how you knew — 'one more than 7 is the next number, 8' — rather than reopening the box.
Try a chain: 'What's one more than 8? And one more than that?' naming each successor without restarting at 1.
Reverse it: 'If I take one back out, how many now?' to practise the predecessor the same way.
activities.intendedInsight: Once you know how many a set has (its cardinality), finding one more is just naming the next counting word — you do not need to recount from one.

activities.title: Reading the staircase and retrieval practice
feedback: Use a reference staircase to confirm answers, but remember a static picture shows the structure for reference and does not itself let the child add or remove one and feel the quantity change; use it alongside enacting the step (on objects or an interactive number track).
For a correct 'one less' answer, affirm that stepping down one place is the mirror of stepping up one.
If an answer treats numbers as growing by an inconsistent amount, return to the single-step model and count along to show each gap is exactly one.
activities.rationale: A labelled staircase and short retrieval prompts consolidate and check the +1/−1 structure after it has been enacted; contrasting a one-step with a two-step move heads off the idea that numbers grow by an inconsistent amount.
sourceClaims: K.CC.4c: 'Understand that each successive number name refers to a quantity that is one larger.'
Year 1: 'given a number, identify 1 more and 1 less'; identify and represent numbers using the number line.
learnerActions: Study a staircase/number track labelled 1..10 and describe how each step compares to the one before.
Point to where 'one more' and 'one less' live relative to a chosen number.
Answer quick fill-in prompts: 'One more than 6 is ___', 'One less than 6 is ___', and 'What number comes next after 8?'
Contrast a single step (+1) with a two-step jump, noticing that a jump of two is not 'one more' (an early taste of skip counting).
activities.intendedInsight: The +1 structure is consistent all along the sequence: every step up is one larger and every step down is one smaller; a fixed staircase can show this structure even though you are not building it yourself.

constraints: Teach 'one more' and 'one less' together as inverse moves on the same model (steps right/left on a number track), not as two unrelated facts.
Do not force counting-on before it emerges: count-from-one dependence is developmental and matures with practice, not a deficit to drill.
Treat the predecessor ('one less') as developing separately from the successor; practise it as its own game rather than assuming backward is automatically as easy as forward.

A static staircase or labelled track supports reference and retrieval but does not itself let the child enact the add-one step or feel the quantity change; pair it with enacting the step, whether on physical objects or an interactive number track.

Fill-in and 'what comes next' prompts are useful retrieval and checking companions but assess recall of the successor; recognising an answer is not the same as enacting the quantity change, so pair them with enacting the +1/−1 step (adding or removing one, on objects or an interactive track).
Concrete objects (cubes, counters, marbles in a box) and screen/number-track models offer different experiences; either can support the step — do not present one as the only possible medium.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Ages 4–6 (Reception/Kindergarten → Year 1). ONE-TO-ONE CORRESPONDENCE — assigning exactly one number-word to each object while counting. The single most central node in the Mathematics taxonomy: the 'how-to-count' foundation every later number concept rests on.
• Standards — UK (DfE): Sits in the EYFS Mathematics programme (Development Matters: 'count objects, actions and sounds'; one-to-one correspondence). No standalone National Curriculum statement — the Year 1 statutory 'count, read and write numbers to 100' assumes accurate object counting; it is the enabling skill, not itself a line of the NC.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): K.CC.4a verbatim — 'When counting objects, say the number names in the standard order, pairing each object with one and only one number name and each number name with one and only one object.' One of Gelman & Gallistel's three 'how-to-count' principles.
• Operational details: Teach TAGGING + KEEPING TRACK — the child must partition the set into 'already counted' vs 'not yet counted' (Thompson). Move/tap each object into a counted pile as it is named; one touch = one word (synchrony). Progress the arrangement: line → array/circle → scattered (hardest — no natural start or track). Start with small sets (≤5) and moveable, tangible objects.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (4–5) counts a line of ≤5 moveable objects, one touch per word, no skips/double-counts. Tier B (5–6) counts ≤10–20 in a line/array AND spots an adult's deliberate skip or double-count. Tier C (6) counts a scattered set to 20 by organising it (lining up / moving counted items) and explains how they avoided recounting.
bestPractices: Teach the 'move-it' method: physically move (or tap) each object into a counted pile so the counted/uncounted partition is visible — Thompson's core requirement for the principle.
Insist on synchrony: one point/touch = one number word; slow the count so the tag and the word land together (rushing causes the classic coordination errors).
Progress the arrangement deliberately: line → array/circle → scattered; scattered sets are the true test because the child must impose their own tracking.
Deliberately model errors (skip one; count one twice) and ask 'did I count right?' — recognising a miscount is diagnostic of the principle.
Keep sets small and objects moveable and tangible (Thompson: tangible/moveable objects help distinguish already-counted from yet-to-be-counted), then build to larger sets.
Count everyday things constantly — stairs, claps, plates (WWC: dedicate time daily and integrate counting throughout the day).
keyRepresentations: Moveable counters + a 'counted' pile / sorting tray (the partition made physical).
Five-frame and ten-frame (structured slots enforce one object per cell).
Fingers — a built-in one-to-one manipulative.
A counting track / row of boxes where each object sits in exactly one box.
Number names spoken in rhythm with points (the aural–motor pairing).
commonMisconceptions: Coordination errors: saying words faster than pointing (or vice versa) → skips or double-counts as the word and the touch drift out of sync.
No tracking strategy on scattered sets → recounting some objects and missing others (the counted/uncounted partition never forms).
Believing pointing without saying (or saying without pointing) still 'counts' — the pairing IS the principle.
Confusing one-to-one correspondence with merely reciting the number-word sequence (stable order): a child can chant '1,2,3,4,5' yet not tag objects one-to-one.

learn.summary: One-to-one correspondence for ages 4–6: assigning exactly one number word to each object while counting, which requires both tagging (one touch = one word, in synchrony) and keeping track (partitioning the set into already-counted vs not-yet-counted). The central learning mechanism is making that partition visible and manipulable — physically moving or tapping each counted object aside — and progressing arrangements from line → array/circle → scattered, where the child must impose their own tracking. Activities combine performing the count, spotting deliberate miscounts, and progressing to organising a scattered set.

activities.title: Feed the squirrel: tap-count a scattered pile
feedback: If the total comes out too high, ask: 'Did any object get two number words? Let's slide each one over as we say its number.'
When a child rushes, slow the count so each touch and each spoken word land together — one touch, one word.
If scattered counting fails, suggest lining the objects up or moving each counted one aside so you can see what is left.
Praise correct reasoning that names WHY: 'You gave each acorn exactly one number and kept the counted ones separate.'
activities.rationale: Thompson identifies the one-one principle as pairing one counting word with each item and partitioning the set into already-counted vs not-yet-counted; tangible, moveable objects help make that distinction, so physically moving counted items makes the core cognitive move visible. An optional interactive version can dim/lock already-counted objects in easy mode and allow double-taps in a challenge mode to let the error surface — this is one proposed way to make the mechanism concrete, not a required or source-proven-superior medium.
sourceClaims: The one-one principle = assigning one and only one counting word to each item; the child must partition the collection into already-counted vs not-yet-counted (tagging + keeping track); tangible, moveable objects help make this distinction.
K.CC.4a: 'When counting objects, say the number names in the standard order, pairing each object with one and only one number name and each number name with one and only one object.'
learnerActions: Count a small pile of objects (e.g. 7 acorns to feed a squirrel) by touching each one exactly once, saying one number word with each touch.
Move or tap each counted object into a 'counted' pile/basket so it is clearly separated from the not-yet-counted objects.
Deliberately rush once and double-tap an object; notice the spoken total becomes wrong (e.g. you say 'eight' even though the basket still holds only 7 acorns).
Tidy the scattered objects into a line and recount, touching each once, so it is easier to get a total you can trust.
When the line count gives the right answer, say aloud why: each object got one word and none was counted twice.
activities.intendedInsight: The rule 'one word per object, and keep track of what you've already counted' is the very difference between a wrong count and a right one; the counted/uncounted split can be made visible and must be maintained.

activities.title: Did Teddy count right? Spot the miscount
feedback: Correct answer: 'No — Teddy counted one button twice, so he said too many. Each button should get just one number word. There are 6.'
If the child accepts '7' because 'he said seven', recount together slowly, sliding each button aside with its single number word so one-word-per-object is visible.

If the child senses it is wrong but cannot locate the double-counted button, replay the count slowly and ask 'Which button did Teddy count twice?' to nudge the monitoring habit — error-monitoring of others' counts develops later, so do not treat this as a misunderstanding to reteach.
Ask probes: 'Which button did Teddy count twice?'; 'If Teddy started from the other end, how many would there be?'; 'What could Teddy do so he doesn't count a button twice?'
activities.rationale: Deliberately modelling errors and asking 'did I count right?' gives useful evidence about the principle: a child who holds the one-word-per-object pairing may reject the count because that pairing broke, while accepting the last word spoken suggests the pairing is not yet the child's rule. Results need cautious reading, because monitoring other people's counts develops later than counting accurately yourself, and recounting to get a different total is itself a legitimate way to detect the error.
sourceClaims: The one-one principle = assigning one and only one counting word to each item; the child must partition the collection into already-counted vs not-yet-counted (tagging + keeping track); tangible, moveable objects help make this distinction.
learnerActions: Watch an adult (or a 'count-with-me' character/puppet) count a set of 6 buttons, deliberately pointing to the SAME button twice (…points to one button saying 'four', points to it again saying 'five', ending on 'seven').
Decide whether the count is right and explain how you know.
Point to exactly which button got two number words.
Recount the set yourself, sliding each button aside as it gets its single number word, and give the correct total (6).
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising a miscount — and locating the specific object that received two words — shows understanding that the word-to-object pairing IS the rule, not just that the last word spoken is the answer.

activities.title: Count everyday things in structured frames and in daily life
feedback: If a child skips or double-counts in a frame, point out that each cell holds exactly one object and should get exactly one word.
For daily counts, keep a steady rhythm so each action gets one number word.
When a scattered set goes wrong, invite the child to line up or move counted items — 'How can you keep track of which ones you've done?'
activities.rationale: Structured representations (five-/ten-frames, counting tracks, fingers) place one object per slot, supporting the one-object-per-word pairing, and the WWC practice guide advises dedicating daily time to maths and integrating counting throughout the day along a developmental progression. Scattered sets require the child to impose their own tracking, making them the harder test of the principle.

learnerActions: Place one object per cell in a five-frame or ten-frame (or a row of boxes), so each object sits in exactly one slot, then count by touching each filled cell once.
Use fingers as a built-in one-to-one tool: raise one finger per counted object.
Count everyday things through the day — stairs as you climb, claps, plates at the table — one number word per step/clap/plate.
Progress from a line, to an array or circle, to a scattered set that you organise yourself before counting.
activities.intendedInsight: One-to-one correspondence applies everywhere and is strengthened by frequent, varied practice; structured slots and fingers support one object per number word (though a child can still skip or double-count cells), and organising a scattered set is the harder test of self-imposed tracking.

constraints: Start with small sets (≤5) of moveable, tangible objects, then build to ≤10–20 and finally scattered sets to 20.
Insist on synchrony: one point/touch = one number word; slow the count so tag and word land together, since rushing causes the classic skip/double-count coordination errors.
Progress arrangements deliberately: line → array/circle → scattered. Scattered sets are hardest because there is no natural start or track.
Distinguish one-to-one correspondence from merely reciting the number-word sequence: a child can chant '1,2,3,4,5' without tagging objects one-to-one.

A static labelled set (each object pre-tagged 1..n) can serve as a reference showing a completed correct count, but it does not let the child perform the one-tap-one-word act, so use it as a reference/scaffold alongside the child counting, not as a substitute.

A multiple-choice or matching task ('how many?' / 'did they count correctly?' / match each object to one numeral) can check recognition and verify whether a count was correct, but does not itself elicit the child's physical one-touch-one-word performance; use it as a retrieval and verification companion alongside, not instead of, the child performing the count.

Point/say coordination lag is a developmental stage, not a misunderstanding — do not drill or verbally correct; slow the pace and have the child physically move each object, which tends to self-correct with the move-it scaffold.
Error-monitoring of others' counts develops later than performing one's own count; a child may reject a wrong total yet be unable to locate the double-counted object.

This is a foundational enabling skill: the statutory Year 1 goal 'count, read and write numbers to 100 in numerals' (National Curriculum in England) assumes accurate object counting but is not itself a line stating one-to-one correspondence.

The WWC practice guide source was marked verified:false in the row; its claim is retained but should be re-checked before relying on it.

The original 'ideal' recommendation (tap-to-count interactive) and its interaction examples (dim/lock already-counted objects, challenge-mode double-tap, tidy-up line-up) are preserved as one concrete, proposed way to make the partition visible, not asserted as the only or best medium; comparative efficacy is not source-established.

Counting-logic self-check: the Teddy diagnostic has 6 buttons but reaches 'seven' because one button receives two number words (one extra word); recounting with one word per button yields 6, so the correct answer (6) and the error explanation are consistent. The acorn scenario (7 acorns, one double-tap → 8) is likewise consistent. No arithmetic errors propagate into learner-facing tasks.

K.CC.4a is cited in activity 1 because it states verbatim the one-object-to-one-number pairing the child performs there; it doubles as standards grounding rather than support for the specific 'move objects to visualise the partition' design choice, which rests on Thompson.

probeDeeper: Can you show me exactly which button Teddy counted twice?
If Teddy started counting from the other end instead, how many buttons would there be?
Count them yourself — slide each button over here as you count it.
What could Teddy do so he doesn't count a button twice?
assess.correctAnswer: No — Teddy counted one button twice, so he said too many. Each button should get just one number word. There are 6.

errorPatterns.pattern: trusts the last word said no matter how the counting went ('he said seven, so there's seven') — thinks the answer is just whatever number you end on
errorPatterns.nextMove: recount together slowly, sliding each button to one side as it gets its single number word, so one-word-per-object is visible
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes, Teddy is right — there are 7.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: accepts Teddy's 7 and, when asked how, repeats 'because he said seven'

errorPatterns.pattern: child's OWN counting shows the point/say lag — fingers and words fall out of step, so a button gets two words or none
errorPatterns.nextMove: do NOT drill or verbally correct — this is a coordination stage, not a misunderstanding; simply slow the pace and have them physically move each object as they count it, and it self-corrects with the move-it scaffold
errorPatterns.revealedBy: when the child counts a fresh set, tags don't line up one-to-one (over- or under-counts)

errorPatterns.pattern: senses the count is wrong but only because recounting gave a different number — cannot point to which button was counted twice
errorPatterns.nextMove: do NOT treat this as a misunderstanding to reteach — error-monitoring of others' counts develops later; simply replay Teddy's count slowly and ask 'which button did Teddy count twice?' to nudge the monitoring habit along
errorPatterns.revealedBy: rejects 7 yet, asked how, says only 'I counted and got 6' without locating the error

responseLevels.gap: Accepts '7' because it was the last word said, or counts a set themselves with skips/double-counts and does not notice.
responseLevels.full: Identifies the specific button that received two number words, explains each object gets exactly one, and counts a fresh set accurately, touching each once.
responseLevels.partial: Says Teddy is wrong and can recount to 6, but cannot locate the double-counted button — rejects the total without seeing the broken one-word-per-object rule.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Watch Teddy count these 6 buttons. (Teddy points to one button, says 'four', then points to the SAME button again and says 'five', ending on 'seven'.) Teddy says there are 7 buttons. Is Teddy right? Tell me how you know.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who holds one-to-one correspondence sees that the word-to-object pairing broke (one button got two words) and says the count is wrong FOR THAT REASON. A child without it either accepts '7' because that was the last word said, or says 'wrong' but can only justify by recounting to a different number — not by locating the double-tagged button. The 'how do you know' tier separates recognising the specific error from merely recounting.

sources.claim: The one-one principle = assigning one and only one counting word to each item; the child must partition the collection into already-counted vs not-yet-counted (tagging + keeping track); tangible, moveable objects help make this distinction.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Representing numbers with objects
topic.description: Represent numbers using objects, pictorial representations, and the number line
evidence: Show a given number using counters, cubes, or fingers
Draw a pictorial representation of a quantity (e.g. tally marks, dots)
Locate a number on a number line
topic.assessmentPrompt: If you ask {{name}} to show you what the number 5 looks like, can they do it in more than one way — such as drawing five dots, holding up five fingers, or pointing to 5 on a number line?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Ages 4–6 (Reception/Kindergarten → Year 1). REPRESENTING NUMBERS multiple ways — with objects, pictures (dots/tallies), and on the NUMBER LINE — and moving between them. A REPRESENTATIONAL topic: the same quantity has many faces and fluency is translating among them. Underpins the concrete–pictorial–abstract (CPA) progression.
• Standards — UK (DfE): NC Year 1 'identify and represent numbers using objects and pictorial representations including the number line'. Extends to Year 2/3 'identify, represent and estimate numbers using different representations, including the number line'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): K.CC.3 'Write numbers from 0 to 20. Represent a number of objects with a written numeral 0–20'. The number-line representation is developed in Grade 1 (1.NBT) and formalised as a number-line diagram in Grade 2 (2.MD.6).
• Operational details: Follow concrete → pictorial → abstract — show a number with counters/cubes/fingers, then draw it (dots, tallies), then locate/mark it on a number line and match to the numeral, keeping the faces side by side. Stress that every face means the SAME quantity. The number line is the pivotal (ordered, spatial, measured) and hardest representation — start with a numbered TRACK (discrete squares) before an empty LINE, and a marked line before a blank one.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (4–5) shows a given number (≤10) with objects/fingers and draws a matching picture. Tier B (5–6) locates a number on a marked 0–20 line and matches object/picture/numeral for the same value. Tier C (6) moves fluently between all four (object ↔ picture ↔ number line ↔ numeral) and explains they are the same amount.
bestPractices: Teach concrete → pictorial → abstract explicitly (CPA): objects, then drawings, then numeral + number line, kept side by side so the links are seen.
Introduce the number line via a numbered TRACK (discrete squares) before a continuous line; a marked line before a blank one.
Always tie every representation back to the quantity ('these all show five') so representations don't become disconnected rituals.
Use varied pictorial forms (dots, tallies, ten-frames) so the child abstracts 'fiveness' from the arrangement rather than a single picture.
Have children CREATE representations, not just read them — draw five, place five on the line, build five with cubes.
keyRepresentations: Counters / cubes / fingers (concrete).
Dots, tally marks, ten-frame (pictorial).
Number track (numbered squares) → number line (marked → blank).
The numeral card (abstract) linked to all of the above.
commonMisconceptions: Treating each representation as a separate task rather than the same quantity in different clothes.
Number-line errors: starting at 1 not 0, or counting the marks/gaps incorrectly; treating the line as a picture rather than a measured, ordered scale (the early 'number-line-as-picture' seed).
Drawing an inexact picture or miscounting tallies so the pictorial doesn't match the quantity.
Believing the numeral is 'the real number' and objects/pictures are not (or vice versa).

learn.summary: For ages 4–6, help children represent the same small quantity (to 20) in multiple ways — concrete objects (counters/cubes/fingers), pictures (dots, tallies, ten-frames), on a number line, and as a numeral — and translate fluently between them, grasping that every face means the SAME amount. Follow concrete → pictorial → abstract (CPA): show, then draw, then locate on the line and match the numeral, keeping the faces side by side. Introduce the number line via a numbered TRACK of discrete squares before a continuous line, and a marked line before a blank one. Have children CREATE representations, not just read them.

activities.title: Five shown four ways, driven from any face
feedback: When the child adds a counter but expects the numeral to stay, show all four faces updating together and ask 'what is the same about all of these now?'

If the child drives from the number line and is surprised the counters change, replay slowly and name the direction they actually moved: for example, 'you moved the marker one step up — so the amount went up by one everywhere' (or 'one step back — so it went down by one everywhere').
Praise naming the shared quantity ('five') rather than just completing the drag.
activities.rationale: Linked, synchronised representations driven from any panel make the CPA bridge something the child causes, countering the misconception that each representation is a separate task. Optional interaction examples (drag a counter, move the marker, live re-forming of the other panels) make the shared-quantity idea concrete; these are illustrative, not required mechanisms.
sourceClaims: Year 1: 'identify and represent numbers using objects and pictorial representations including the number line'; Years 2–3 'identify, represent and estimate numbers using different representations, including the number line'.
The concrete–pictorial–abstract (CPA) progression and multiple linked representations build number sense; the number line is a key structural representation introduced via a numbered track.
learnerActions: Set a small number (to 20) and see it at once as counters, a dotty picture (or tally/ten-frame), a point on a number line, and the numeral card.
Add or remove one counter and watch the picture gain or lose a dot, the number-line marker move one step, and the numeral change to match.
Drive the change from a DIFFERENT face: slide the number-line marker, or add a tally, and watch the other three faces re-form to match.
Say aloud 'these all show ___' each time, naming the quantity after a change.
Switch the number line between numbered-track mode (discrete squares) and continuous-line mode, and between a marked line and a blank one.
activities.intendedInsight: A quantity has many faces — blocks, dots, a spot on the line, a symbol — and when the amount changes, every face must change to match, because they all show the same amount in different clothing.

activities.title: Build it, draw it, place it (child creates every face)
feedback: If the drawn picture has the wrong count, draw and count together, one mark per count word, then lay the drawn marks beside the counters to check they match.
If the child writes the digit shape when asked to draw the quantity, point out 'the symbol tells us the number, but a picture shows how many — draw that many dots.'

If the child can build with counters but stalls on the line, lay the counters ALONG the number line, one in each unit space starting from 0 (between 0 and 1, between 1 and 2, and so on), so the far end of the last counter lines up with the number's mark; then count the jumps from 0 to check.
activities.rationale: Creating representations (not only reading them) is a stated best practice and exposes the 'draw the symbol not the quantity' and 'can produce in one mode only' error patterns so they can be addressed.
sourceClaims: K.CC.3: 'Write numbers from 0 to 20. Represent a number of objects with a written numeral 0–20 (with 0 representing a count of no objects).'

Year 1: 'identify and represent numbers using objects and pictorial representations including the number line'; Years 2–3 'identify, represent and estimate numbers using different representations, including the number line'.
learnerActions: Given a target number (≤10 for younger children, to 20 later), build it with counters or cubes — fingers work well for numbers up to ten.
Draw a matching picture — exactly that many dots or tally marks, one mark per count word.
Locate and mark the number on a number line, counting the JUMPS from 0 aloud.
Match the numeral card to the set, the picture, and the number-line point, saying they all show the same amount.
activities.intendedInsight: The child can PRODUCE a quantity in every mode, not just recognise it, and sees that the picture and number-line point carry the amount just as the objects do.

activities.title: Read the dot: count the jumps from 0
feedback: If the child reads 6 as 5 or 7, hop a finger from 0 counting the jumps aloud, labelling 0 explicitly as the start, not 'one'.
Confirm: 'the dot is 6 steps on from 0, so it marks 6.'
Ask 'where would 7 be? how do you know?' to check the jump-counting generalises.
activities.rationale: Off-by-one errors come from counting ticks instead of the gaps between them, or treating 0 as the first count; counting jumps from a labelled 0 targets this directly. The number line is the ordered, spatial, measured representation and the hardest, so it is introduced via a numbered track and a marked line precedes a blank one.
sourceClaims: The concrete–pictorial–abstract (CPA) progression and multiple linked representations build number sense; the number line is a key structural representation introduced via a numbered track.
learnerActions: Look at a number line from 0 to 10 with a dot marked on 6; point to the dot and say what number it means and how you know.
Count the JUMPS from 0 aloud, hopping a finger from 0, rather than counting the ticks.
Point to 0 and say what 0 means here — the start, not a step.
Then show the same number with counters and draw a matching picture.
activities.intendedInsight: A number-line point is read by counting the steps from 0, which is the start and not itself a step; 0 anchors the measured, ordered scale.

activities.title: Reference wall and match checks
feedback: For a correct match, ask the child to justify: 'how do you know that one shows 5?'
When a tap-reveal names a face, prompt the child to find the same quantity in another face before moving on.
activities.rationale: A static tap-to-reveal reference and matching/placing tasks are a good naming and assessment layer across representations; they support recognition but on their own do not elicit the independent construction and translation that the build/draw/place activity provides.
learnerActions: Use a 'number shown four ways' reference the child can tap to name each face (tap the number-line point → 'five'; tap the tally → 'five').
Answer 'which shows 5?' matching tasks across objects, pictures, number line, and numeral.
Use a slider to place a number on the line, or draw a path to mark it.
Discuss probe questions: 'You drew 6 dots and here are 6 counters — how are they the same? how are they different?' and 'If I show you 4 fingers, can you put a dot on the line for that number?'
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to name and match each face is a useful naming/reference layer that supports, but does not replace, building and translating for oneself.

constraints: Keep all faces (objects, picture, number line, numeral) side by side and always tie each back to the quantity ('these all show five') so representations don't become disconnected rituals.
Introduce the number line via a numbered TRACK (discrete squares) before a continuous line, and a marked line before a blank one; the number line is the hardest, measured, ordered representation.
Use varied pictorial forms (dots, tallies, ten-frames) so the child abstracts 'fiveness' from the arrangement rather than memorising one picture.

Recognition-only tasks (tap-to-reveal, 'which shows 5?' matching) assess and name but do not by themselves show the child can independently construct or translate a quantity; pair them with build/draw/place work.

Tier the demand: 4–5 shows a number ≤10 with objects/fingers and draws a matching picture; 5–6 locates on a marked 0–20 line and matches object/picture/numeral; 6 moves fluently among all four and explains they are the same amount.

A static reference image cannot itself let the child create or translate a quantity, so use it as a companion rather than the main teaching activity — this is a scope note about that specific scaffold's affordance, not a claim that static images cannot teach.

Where would 7 be on the line? How do you know?
If I show you 4 fingers, can you put a dot on the line for that number?
Point to 0 — what does 0 mean here?
assess.correctAnswer: The dot marks 6 — it's 6 steps on from 0. (Places/counts out exactly 6 counters.) (Draws 6 dots or tally marks.) Each way shows the same amount: six.

errorPatterns.pattern: number-line off-by-one — reads the marked point as 5 or 7 because they count the 0 tick as 'one', or count marks instead of the jumps between them
errorPatterns.nextMove: count the JUMPS from 0 aloud, hopping a finger from 0; label 0 explicitly as the start, not a step
errorPatterns.revealedBy: names the wrong number for the dot; starts the count at the 0 mark saying 'one'

errorPatterns.pattern: draws the symbol, not the quantity — asked to draw 6, writes the digit '6' or makes a vague scatter of marks rather than exactly six items
errorPatterns.nextMove: draw-and-count together, one mark per count word, then match the drawn set back to the 6 counters so the picture is seen to carry the amount
errorPatterns.revealedBy: the picture's count isn't 6, or the child draws the numeral shape

errorPatterns.pattern: can produce in one mode only — shows 6 counters fine but can't locate 6 on the line (or vice versa); treats each representation as a separate skill, not the same number
errorPatterns.nextMove: lay the counters ALONG the number line so position and quantity line up side by side, bridging the two representations — the quantity idea is there, only the link is missing
errorPatterns.revealedBy: succeeds in one representation and stalls when asked to translate to another

responseLevels.gap: Translations don't preserve quantity — miscounts the number-line point, or draws the numeral / a wrong number of marks unrelated to the target.
responseLevels.full: Reads the marked point as the right number, produces the same quantity with counters and in a drawing, and explains that all three show the same amount.
responseLevels.partial: Represents the number correctly in one mode (e.g. counters) but falters translating to another — mislocates it on the line or is off-by-one — treating the representations as separate.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a number line from 0 to 10 with a dot marked on 6. Point to the dot and tell me what number it means and how you know. Now show me that same number using these counters. Last, draw me a picture that shows that number.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands the representations maps all three — number-line position, counters, drawing — to the same quantity, treating them as the same number in different clothes. A child without it mislocates the point (counts the 0 tick as 'one', giving 5 or 7), draws the numeral shape or a wrong number of marks, or produces counters unrelated to the target: the translations don't preserve quantity. Requiring both an INTERPRET (read the dot) and two TRANSLATES (counters, drawing) exposes exactly where the mapping breaks.
