topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Counting objects to 20
topic.description: Count a set of objects to answer 'how many?' for sets up to 20 (arranged in lines, arrays, circles, or scattered)
evidence: Accurately count up to 20 objects in a line
Count up to 10 scattered objects without losing track
Given a number 1–20, count out that many objects from a larger set
topic.assessmentPrompt: If you spread out 15 buttons on the table in a random arrangement and ask {{name}} how many there are, can they count them all carefully and give you the right answer?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Ages 5–6 (Reception/Year 1). COUNTING OBJECTS TO 20 — applying one-to-one correspondence AND cardinality to answer 'how many?' for sets up to 20 in any arrangement (line, array, circle, scattered), and counting out a given number (give-N). Where the counting principles become a reliable procedure.
• Standards — UK (DfE): NC Year 1 'count, read and write numbers to 100 in numerals' and 'read and write numbers from 1 to 20 in numerals and words'. Underpinned by EYFS object counting; teen numbers (11–19) as 'ten and some more' bridge to place value.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): K.CC.5 verbatim — 'Count to answer "how many?" questions about as many as 20 things arranged in a line, a rectangular array, or a circle, or as many as 10 things in a scattered configuration; given a number from 1–20, count out that many objects.'
• Operational details: Combine one-to-one (tag each once) with cardinality (last word = total). Arrangement matters: line/array/circle are easier (a natural order exists); SCATTERED is hardest — the child must impose tracking (move counted items aside, or count round systematically). Give-N (count out exactly N) is the stronger check. Use the TEN-FRAME so teens read as a full ten + extras ('ten and three' = 13), seeding place value.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (5) counts a line of up to 20 accurately and counts ≤10 scattered by organising them. Tier B (5–6) counts 20 in any arrangement and gives-N up to 20. Tier C (6) counts a scattered 20 with a self-chosen tracking strategy and reads a teen set on a ten-frame as 'ten and __'.
bestPractices: Insist on a tracking strategy for scattered sets — move each counted object aside, or count along a consistent path — so nothing is missed or double-counted.
Use give-N ('count out 13') as the strongest assessment — harder than 'how many?' and it exposes shaky cardinality.
Introduce the ten-frame for teens: fill a ten, then extras, so 14 is seen as 'ten and four' (early place value, not a mystery word).
Vary the arrangement deliberately (line → array → circle → scattered) so counting is robust to layout and the 'different arrangement = different number' error is defeated.
Keep objects moveable and connect the count to the written numeral and the spoken 'altogether'.
keyRepresentations: Ten-frames (one full + a partial for teens).
Moveable counters + a 'counted' tray.
Sets shown in line / array / circle / scattered (a deliberate arrangement ladder).
A numeral card matched to the counted set.
commonMisconceptions: Losing track on scattered sets → skips or double-counts (no tracking strategy).
Recounting when asked 'how many?' (cardinality not secure) or miscounting across the teens.
Treating teen numbers as unanalysable words rather than 'ten and some ones'.
Believing a rearranged set has a different total (conservation).

learn.summary: Ages 5–6 (Reception/Year 1) counting objects to 20: coordinating one-to-one correspondence (tag each item exactly once) with cardinality (the last count word is the total) to answer 'how many?' for sets in any arrangement — line, array, circle, or scattered — and to count out a given number (give-N). Scattered sets are hardest because the child must impose a tracking strategy; give-N is the strongest check of cardinality. Ten-frames help teen numbers read as 'ten and some more', seeding place value. (The cited standard specifies scattered configurations up to 10 and ordered arrangements up to 20.)

activities.title: Organise and count a scattered set
feedback: If repeat counts give different totals, something went wrong in at least one count. Often counted and uncounted items got mixed up, but a number word may also have been skipped, or the words and pointing may have got out of step. Listen to the number sequence, and try physically moving each one aside as you count: 'move each one over here as you count it.'
If asked 'how many?' and the child recounts from the start, prompt: 'You just counted — what was the last number? That tells us how many.'
Ask: 'How could you count the scattered ones so you don't lose your place?' to prompt a self-chosen strategy rather than supplying one every time.
Rearrange the same counters and ask how many now — the total should not change because nothing was added or removed.
activities.rationale: One-to-one and cardinal principles must be coordinated to enumerate reliably, and moveable objects let a child physically track counted versus uncounted. Scattered arrangements demand a self-imposed strategy, which develops with practice rather than reteaching the count. The standard specifies scattered sets to 10; counting ~20 scattered is a harder extension drawn from the original Tier C.
sourceClaims: K.CC.5 verbatim: 'Count to answer "how many?" questions about as many as 20 things arranged in a line, a rectangular array, or a circle, or as many as 10 things in a scattered configuration; given a number from 1–20, count out that many objects.'
One-one plus cardinal principles must be coordinated to reliably enumerate a set; tangible moveable objects help track counted vs uncounted.
learnerActions: Start with a small scattered pile (up to 10) of moveable counters or buttons spread randomly.
Count them by moving each counted item aside into a 'counted' tray (or sliding it along a consistent path) so counted and uncounted are clearly separated.
Say how many there are altogether, then recount and check you get the same number.
Repeat with a larger scattered set of up to 20 counters (a harder extension), choosing your own tracking path.
Match a numeral card to the final count.
activities.intendedInsight: A chaotic scatter becomes reliably countable by imposing order — moving each item as you count it so nothing is skipped or counted twice — and the last number you say is how many there are, no matter how the objects are arranged.

activities.title: Count out exactly N (give-N)
feedback: If the child counts past the target or hands over the whole pile, they are not yet using the number as a stop signal — state the target, count into a cupped hand, and do a stop-and-check: 'how many do we need? tell me when to stop.'
Follow up with 'Give me 4 more — now how many?' to link counting-on to the running total.
Praise stopping at exactly the right item, not just producing counters.
activities.rationale: Give-N is harder than 'how many?' because it requires holding a target while counting; it exposes shaky cardinality that a plain count can hide. Stopping at the target rebuilds the last-word-as-total link.
sourceClaims: K.CC.5 verbatim: 'Count to answer "how many?" questions about as many as 20 things arranged in a line, a rectangular array, or a circle, or as many as 10 things in a scattered configuration; given a number from 1–20, count out that many objects.'
learnerActions: From a large pile, count out exactly a requested number (e.g. 'give me 13') into a cupped hand or small tray.
Say the target first, then count one item at a time, stopping when you reach it.
Check: 'How many did we need? Tell me when to stop' — point and count together to confirm you stopped at the target.
Try a round with a teen target such as 16, then compare counting out from different-sized piles.
activities.intendedInsight: Counting out a specific quantity means using the target number as a stop signal — you hold the goal in mind while counting, which is cardinality in action and a stronger test than simply reporting 'how many'.

activities.title: Vary the arrangement to make counting robust
feedback: If a child expects a different total after rearranging, slowly rearrange in front of them and recount together: nothing was added or taken away, so it stays the same.
Ask: 'If you started counting the line from the other end, how many?' to challenge the idea that direction changes the total.

Lines and arrays have a natural order to follow. Circles have an order too, but no natural start or end, so the child must mark or remember where they began to avoid counting items twice. Scattered sets need a strategy the child imposes. Name these differences so the child knows when extra care is needed.
activities.rationale: Deliberately varying arrangement makes counting robust to layout and challenges the belief that a different arrangement means a different number. Lines and arrays offer a natural order. A circle offers an order but no natural starting point, so the start must be marked. Scattered sets require imposed tracking. The conservation point — same total after rearranging — is a reasonable curricular inference and is not directly asserted by the cited standard.
sourceClaims: K.CC.5 verbatim: 'Count to answer "how many?" questions about as many as 20 things arranged in a line, a rectangular array, or a circle, or as many as 10 things in a scattered configuration; given a number from 1–20, count out that many objects.'
learnerActions: Count the same quantity shown four ways in turn: a line, a rectangular array, a circle, and scattered.
After counting a neat line, count it again starting from the other end and check the total is the same.
Count an array along rows, then along columns, and confirm the total does not change.
State each total aloud with 'altogether' and match it to the written numeral.
activities.intendedInsight: The total depends only on the objects, not on how they are laid out or which end you start from — a rearranged set still has the same number.

activities.title: Read teen numbers on a ten-frame as 'ten and some more'
feedback: If a teen is treated as an unanalysable word, point to the full frame and the extras: 'a full ten, and three more — thirteen.'
If the count across the teens slips, slow down and fill one frame completely before starting the extras.
Connect the spoken 'ten and four', the filled ten-frame, and the numeral 14 so all three line up.
activities.rationale: Ten-frames show teen numbers as ten-and-ones, which seeds place value and helps a child stop treating teens as random words. Note: the ten-frame source for this claim is marked unverified in the row and was not re-verified in this rewrite.
sourceClaims: Ten-frames represent teen numbers as ten-and-ones, seeding place value.
learnerActions: Count a teen quantity (11–19) by filling a ten-frame completely first, then placing the extras in a second frame.
Say the number as 'ten and three… thirteen' so the full ten and the extras are both visible.
Match the ten-frame picture to the written numeral (e.g. 13).
Repeat with other teen numbers, each time noticing the full ten plus a few more.
activities.intendedInsight: A teen number is not a mysterious word — it is a full ten with a few more ones, which is the beginning of place value.

activities.title: Spot and fix a miscount (optional Socratic check)
feedback: If the child misses the error, slow the demonstration down and point at the item that was skipped or double-counted.
Encourage them to name the fix ('move each one over as you count') rather than only saying 'it's wrong'.
activities.rationale: Fixing another's miscount may have mild Socratic value for articulating counting principles, but the core skill is an enacted count, so this supplements rather than replaces hands-on counting. Its efficacy is proposed, not validated.
sourceClaims: One-one plus cardinal principles must be coordinated to reliably enumerate a set; tangible moveable objects help track counted vs uncounted.
learnerActions: Watch (or listen to) a puppet or partner count a scattered pile, deliberately skipping one item or counting one twice.
Decide whether the count was right, explain what went wrong, and show how to count it correctly using a tracking strategy.
Suggest what the puppet should do differently next time (e.g. move each item aside).
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to catch and explain a counting slip shows you understand why one-to-one tagging and tracking matter — not just how to recite numbers.

constraints: The core objective is an enacted count: the child must physically tag, track, and count out objects. Recognition-only tasks (choosing 'how many?' from options, judging a shown count) can assess or supplement but do not by themselves elicit the independent counting and give-N that is the point.
A labelled, already-counted set can serve as a reference example but cannot enact the count or the give-N task; use it only as a scaffold.
Give-N (count out exactly N) is a stronger check of cardinality than 'how many?' — include it, not just set-reporting.
Scattered-set tracking is a developing habit: if a child loses track, model a strategy (move each item aside) rather than reteaching counting as though the concept is absent.
Keep objects moveable and connect each count to the spoken total ('altogether') and the written numeral.

If an on-screen version is used, features like tap-to-count lockout (a counted item cannot be tapped again), a 'tidy into a line/ten-frame' helper, a drag-out give-N mode, and a persistent total badge can make the mechanism concrete — these are optional illustrations, not required mechanisms, and should not replace hands-on counting with physical objects.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are 17 counters in a line — count them and tell me how many. Now here are 10 counters scattered on the table — count these. pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Ages 5–7 (Year 1 → Year 2). SKIP COUNTING in 2s, 5s and 10s — the first move beyond counting by ones into counting equal GROUPS. The gateway to multiplication (equal groups / repeated addition), even numbers, telling time (5s) and place value (10s).
• Standards — UK (DfE): NC Year 1 'count in multiples of 2s, 5s and 10s'; guidance: 'counting in 2s, 5s and 10s from different multiples to develop their recognition of patterns in the number system (for example, odd and even numbers).'
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): K.CC.1 'count … by tens'; Grade 2 extends — 2.NBT.2 'Count within 1000; skip-count by 5s, 10s, and 100s.' Skip counting underpins the multiplication foundations of 2.OA.3–4 and Grade 3 OA.
• Operational details: Teach as counting equal GROUPS, not a new chant — each 'step' is one more group of 2/5/10 (link to repeated addition, the multiplication seed). Use the HUNDRED SQUARE (shade 5s → two columns; 10s → one column; 2s → even columns) and the NUMBER LINE (equal jumps landing on multiples) so the pattern is seen. Count from different starting multiples, not only 0. Anchor 2s↔even, 5s↔clock/tallies/fingers, 10s↔place value.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (5–6) counts in 10s to 100 and 2s to 20 from 0. Tier B (6) counts in 5s to 50 and links 2s to even numbers. Tier C (6–7) counts in 2s/5s/10s from a non-zero multiple and explains each step adds a group ('5s go up by five each time = one more group of five').
bestPractices: Teach each skip count as adding one equal GROUP (repeated addition), not a disconnected chant — this is the multiplication seed.
Shade multiples on a hundred square so the visual pattern (columns/diagonals) makes the sequence predictable rather than memorised.
Use a number line with equal-sized jumps landing on multiples — the jump size IS the step, making 'counting in 5s' concrete.
Count from different starting multiples and in both directions so it is flexible, not a fixed rote song.
Anchor to real contexts: 2s (pairs, even numbers), 5s (fingers, tally marks, clock minutes), 10s (tens, money).
keyRepresentations: Hundred square with multiples shaded (pattern by column/diagonal).
Number line with equal jumps (the jump = the step size).
Equal groups / arrays of 2, 5, 10 (the bridge to multiplication).
Fingers (5s/10s), tally marks (5s), coins (5s/10s).
commonMisconceptions: Reciting the multiples as a chant with no sense that each step is +one group — so it doesn't transfer to multiplication.
Thinking the multiples are the ONLY numbers that 'exist', or that skip counting removes the in-between numbers (7 isn't 'skipped away').
Only able to start from 0 — can't skip-count from a different multiple or backwards.
Confusing 'counting in 2s' with 'counting to 2', or losing the pattern at decade boundaries (5s: '…45, 50, 55').

learn.summary: Skip counting in 2s, 5s and 10s for ages 5–7, taught as counting equal GROUPS (one more group of 2/5/10 each step) rather than a memorised chant — the bridge to multiplication, repeated addition, even numbers, clock minutes and place value. Core representations are the hundred square (on a standard 10-wide square, shaded multiples of 2, 5 and 10 form straight column patterns) and the number line (equal-sized jumps landing on multiples). Learners should count from different starting multiples and in both directions, not only forward from 0.

activities.title: One hop, one group: linking jumps, counters and the hundred square
feedback: If a learner recites fluently from 0 but can't say what comes after 40 in 10s, bring them back to one jump: 'each hop adds ten — show me the next group.'
When the shaded 10s form a single straight column and the 5s two columns, prompt: 'what do you notice about where they are?' so the pattern, not memory, drives the next number.

If a learner sub-counts the in-between numbers under their breath, that is a normal developing step — let the equal jump and the shaded pattern gradually make it feel like one move; do not mark it wrong.
If starting at 30 they restart from 0, say 'start here and keep hopping' and practise entering mid-sequence from several multiples.
activities.rationale: Showing the jump, the stacked group of counters and the shaded hundred-square cells together makes 'counting in fives' concrete as repeated equal groups rather than a chant, and counting from varied multiples and in both directions keeps it flexible. Linked, simultaneously-moving views (number line + counters + hundred square) are offered as one way to make the group structure visible; the panels moving together is an optional interaction example, not a required mechanism.
sourceClaims: Year 1: 'count in multiples of 2s, 5s and 10s'; guidance: counting in 2s, 5s and 10s from different multiples to develop recognition of number patterns (e.g. odd and even).
2.NBT.2 'Count within 1000; skip-count by 5s, 10s, and 100s'; skip counting underpins multiplication foundations (equal groups / repeated addition).
Skip counting is taught as counting equal groups (the multiplication bridge) using the hundred square and number line to make patterns visible.
learnerActions: Pick which step size you are counting in: 2, 5 or 10.
Take one step forward on a number line, making an equal-sized jump (a jump of 5 for 5s) that lands on the next multiple.
For each jump, add a GROUP of that many counters into a new stack/tower, so you see the jump as 'one more group of five'.
Shade or light up the cells you land on (5, 10, 15 …) on a hundred square as you go.
Say aloud what each step adds: 'each hop adds five — one more group of five.'
Try starting from a non-zero multiple (e.g. start at 30 and count on in 10s: 30, 40, 50 …).
Try counting in the other direction too (e.g. count back in 10s from 50: 50, 40, 30 …).
activities.intendedInsight: Each step of skip counting adds (or, going back, removes) one equal group, so the next multiple can be predicted from the pattern and from 'one more group' instead of recited — this is the seed of multiplication and repeated addition.

activities.title: Spotting the pattern on a multiples chart
feedback: If a learner says the multiples are the 'only numbers that exist' or that in-between numbers are 'skipped away', point to the chart: 7 is still there, we are just landing on every second/fifth/tenth number.
At a decade boundary, if they lose the pattern (…45, 50, 55), have them trace the column to confirm the next landing cell.
activities.rationale: A pre-marked multiples chart is a genuinely useful reference whose pattern is visible even when static; it supports recognising multiples and crossing decade boundaries. It shows the pattern but does not itself require the learner to generate each step, so pair it with tasks where the learner constructs and explains steps.
sourceClaims: Year 1: 'count in multiples of 2s, 5s and 10s'; guidance: counting in 2s, 5s and 10s from different multiples to develop recognition of number patterns (e.g. odd and even).
learnerActions: Look at a hundred square or multiples chart with the 2s, 5s or 10s already marked.
Tap or point to a multiple to reveal it and the group it stands for (e.g. 15 = three groups of five).
Describe the visual pattern: 10s make one straight column, 5s make two columns, 2s shade the even columns.
Use the chart as a reference to answer 'what comes next in 5s after 45?' across a decade boundary.
activities.intendedInsight: The multiples sit in a predictable visual pattern, so you can find the next one by reading the pattern rather than restarting the chant — and the pattern survives decade boundaries like 45, 50, 55.

activities.title: Anchoring 2s, 5s and 10s to real things
feedback: If a learner confuses 'counting in 2s' with 'counting to 2', re-ground in pairs: each new pair adds two to the total.
Use fingers and tally marks to re-establish the fives if the 5s pattern slips.
activities.rationale: Anchoring each step size to familiar contexts gives meaning to the groups and supports transfer to even numbers, telling time and place value.
sourceClaims: Year 1: 'count in multiples of 2s, 5s and 10s'; guidance: counting in 2s, 5s and 10s from different multiples to develop recognition of number patterns (e.g. odd and even).
learnerActions: Count pairs of objects in 2s and connect to even numbers (2, 4, 6 …).
Count hands/fingers and tally marks in 5s (5, 10, 15 …) and clock minutes in 5s.
Count groups of ten — tens blocks or 10p coins — in 10s and link to place value (how many tens).
Say how each context shows 'one more group': one more pair, one more hand of five, one more ten.
activities.intendedInsight: Skip counting describes real repeated groups — pairs, fives and tens — so 2s↔even, 5s↔clock/tallies/fingers, 10s↔place value make the counts meaningful and memorable.

activities.title: Fluency practice: fill, continue, match
feedback: A 'next multiple' or 'fill the gap' task checks fluency but, on its own, may let a learner answer by recognition; follow up with 'how did you know?' to check for group reasoning.
In the oral partner game, use the caught slip to prompt 'how did you know that was wrong?' rather than just correcting.
activities.rationale: These tasks give targeted fluency practice and the array-matching links sequences back to equal groups. Fill/continue tasks check recall and recognition but do not by themselves show the learner is reasoning from groups, so pair them with the construction and explanation tasks. The oral call-and-response gives fluency and listening practice but lacks a seen pattern, so it complements rather than replaces the visual work.
learnerActions: Fill in a missing multiple in a sequence (…, 10, __, 20 in 5s).
Say what comes next in 2s/5s/10s from a given number, including across a decade boundary.
Put a set of multiples in order.
Match a skip-count (e.g. 5, 10, 15) to an array or picture of equal groups.
Do an oral count-in-5s with a partner as call-and-response, and catch a deliberate slip in the other person's count.
activities.intendedInsight: Repeated varied practice — including continuing from non-zero starts and matching counts to equal-group arrays — builds fluency while keeping the count tied to groups.

constraints: Teach skip counting as adding one equal group each step (repeated addition), not as a disconnected chant — this is the multiplication seed.
Count from different starting multiples (not only 0) and in both directions, so the skill is flexible rather than a fixed rote song.

A pre-marked multiples chart and fill/continue practice items are references and recognition checks; they show or test the pattern but do not require the learner to independently construct each step, so pair them with tasks where the learner generates and explains steps.

Reverting to counting the in-between numbers by ones, and difficulty starting from a non-zero multiple, are developmental stages that improve with practice — do not mark them as errors; scaffold with equal jumps and hundred-square patterns.
Do not imply that only the multiples 'exist' or that in-between numbers are removed; the full number sequence is still present, we just land on every 2nd/5th/10th number.
Watch decade boundaries in 5s (…45, 50, 55) where the pattern is easily lost.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy framing of one interactive as 'the killer move' / 'the insight clicks' was softened: the linked number-line/counters/hundred-square views are presented as one effective way to make equal groups visible, not as uniquely necessary.

The oral call-and-response and static chart are described by narrow affordances (fluency/listening practice; visible but non-generative reference); no categorical 'only this teaches' or 'cannot teach' claim is asserted.
Catalog/product vocabulary ('quiz', artefact-fit rankings) was removed from learner-facing text; where mentioned in these notes it only documents the removal.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Ages 5–6 (Reception/Year 1). ROTE COUNTING to 100 — reciting the number-word sequence fluently, forwards and backwards, from 0, 1, or any given number, by ones. Gelman & Gallistel's STABLE-ORDER principle in action; the verbal spine that object counting, place value and skip counting all run on.
• Standards — UK (DfE): NC Year 1 verbatim — 'count to and across 100, forwards and backwards, beginning with 0 or 1, or from any given number'. Non-statutory guidance distinguishes 'counting as reciting numbers' from 'counting as enumerating objects'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): K.CC.1 'Count to 100 by ones and by tens'; K.CC.2 'Count forward beginning from a given number within the known sequence (instead of having to begin at 1).'
• Operational details: Build a stable ordered list at least as long as needed (Thompson: you can't count seven items if your names stop at six). Target the two hard spots — the irregular TEENS (eleven, twelve, thirteen, not 'oneteen') and the DECADE BOUNDARIES (…28, 29 → 30; 39 → 40) where children stall or invent 'twenty-ten'. Backward counting and starting mid-sequence are harder and must be practised explicitly. Use the HUNDRED SQUARE to expose the repeating 0–9 ones pattern down each column so counting becomes pattern, not just memory.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (5) rote counts forward 0→~30 without skipping/repeating and recites the teens correctly. Tier B (5–6) counts to 100 forward and back from 20→0, bridging decade boundaries. Tier C (6) starts a forward OR backward count from any given number (e.g. 'from 67') and predicts the number after a decade boundary.
bestPractices: Practise oral counting daily and rhythmically (chants, songs, choral counting); little and often builds the stable list.
Target decade boundaries and irregular teens explicitly — rehearse '…29, 30…' and '…39, 40…' as named hurdles where the sequence breaks down.
Practise BACKWARD counting and starting from any number separately (much harder than forward-from-one) — essential for later counting-back subtraction.
Use a hundred square / number track so the ones-digit cycle (0–9 repeating) and the new-row-per-decade structure are SEEN, converting recall into prediction.
Distinguish reciting the sequence from counting objects — keep both, but name which you are doing.
keyRepresentations: Hundred square (rows of ten; a column shares a ones digit).
Number track / number line 0–100.
Counting songs, rhymes and choral chant (the aural sequence).
A pointer/marker moving along the track as the class counts.
commonMisconceptions: Decade-boundary stalls: '…28, 29, twenty-ten' or jumping to the wrong decade — the ones-cycle-to-next-ten transition isn't secured.
Irregular teens: 'eleventeen', or mapping teen words to the wrong quantity; hearing 'thirteen' as 30.
Counting forward from one but not backward or from a mid-point — the sequence is stored as a single forward chant.
Confusing rote reciting with meaningful counting — chanting numbers with nothing attached and assuming that IS counting.

learn.summary: Ages 5–6 (Reception/Year 1) rote counting to (and across) 100: reciting the number-word sequence fluently by ones — forwards and backwards, beginning from 0, 1, or any given number. The aim is to build a stable, repeatable ordered list of number words that object counting, place value and skip counting later run on, while distinguishing reciting the sequence from counting objects. Target the two predictable break points: the irregular teens (eleven, twelve, thirteen — not 'oneteen') and the decade boundaries (…28, 29 → 30; …39 → 40). Backward counting and starting mid-sequence are harder than forward-from-one and must be practised explicitly. A hundred square exposes the repeating 0–9 ones pattern so counting becomes prediction, not pure memory.

activities.title: Predict across the decade boundary on a hundred square
feedback: If a learner says 'twenty-ten' or 'sixty-ten' at a boundary, do NOT re-drill the whole 1–100 sequence. Target just the seam where the error happened (e.g. 68, 69, 70 for 'sixty-ten'; 28, 29, 30 for 'twenty-ten'), plus similar seams such as 38, 39, 40, until each bridge is automatic.

If a learner jumps to the wrong decade (…39, 50), show that after 39 the count moves to the next ten, 40, not 50. Point to where 40 sits on the chart being used: on a 1–100 square it is the last cell of the 31–40 row, and 50 ends the row below; on a 0–99 square 40 starts its row. Ask which number comes straight after 39, so the learner sees that the tens go up by just one ten.
When a prediction is correct, name the pattern aloud: 'the ones went 7, 8, 9 and then started again at 0, and the tens went up by one ten.'
activities.rationale: Decade boundaries and irregular teen words are the predictable places the oral sequence breaks down; a hundred square makes the repeating ones-cycle and ten-per-row decade structure visible, which can turn recall into prediction. A visible marker, forward/back movement, start-anywhere entry and optional say-back audio make the counting mechanism concrete; these are illustrative interactions, not required ones — a static hundred square or a paper number track pointed at cell by cell can serve the same teaching purpose with less automation.
sourceClaims: Year 1 verbatim: 'count to and across 100, forwards and backwards, beginning with 0 or 1, or from any given number'; guidance distinguishes counting as reciting from counting as enumerating objects.
Decade boundaries and irregular teen words are the predictable break points in the oral sequence; the hundred square exposes the repeating structure.
learnerActions: Point to a chosen starting cell on a hundred square (e.g. 67) and count on aloud, moving a pointer or marker cell by cell: '68, 69…'
As you approach a decade boundary, pause and predict the next number BEFORE saying it ('after 69 comes…?') and check whether the tens goes up by one ten (to 70) rather than inventing 'sixty-ten'.
Trace down a single column and say the numbers aloud to notice the ones digit stays the same while the tens digit climbs.
Repeat for the rehearsed seams: 28, 29, 30 and 38, 39, 40, until each bridge is automatic.
Then run the marker the other way to count backward across a boundary (e.g. 41, 40, 39…).
activities.intendedInsight: 100 numbers are not 100 separate things to memorise: the ones digits cycle through 0–9 again and again (on a 1–100 square each row runs from 1 to 10, e.g. 31–40; on a 0–99 square from 0 to 9, e.g. 40–49). So once you know the repeating ones pattern, the decade words and the irregular teens, and can cross cleanly into the next ten, most of the sequence becomes predictable.

activities.title: Start anywhere and keep going
feedback: If a learner restarts at 1 when asked to begin at 23, do NOT treat it as an error to penalise — it matures with practice; play 'start here and keep going' from many points using a visible track.

If backward counting is halting, skips, or reverts to forward, do NOT expect it to arrive alongside forward counting. Practise short backward runs separately with a number line before building up to 20→0, then to longer backward runs from any given number up to 100.
Keep runs short and slow when the word string itself is insecure; point to each number rather than drilling at speed.
activities.rationale: Starting mid-sequence and counting backward develop separately from, and later than, forward-from-one counting, so they warrant explicit dedicated practice; backward counting also underpins later counting-back subtraction. A number line or track gives a visible referent for entry points and direction.
sourceClaims: Year 1 verbatim: 'count to and across 100, forwards and backwards, beginning with 0 or 1, or from any given number'; guidance distinguishes counting as reciting from counting as enumerating objects.
K.CC.1 'Count to 100 by ones and by tens'; K.CC.2 'Count forward beginning from a given number within the known sequence (instead of having to begin at 1).'
learnerActions: On being given a starting number (e.g. 'start at 23'), begin the count there and continue forward WITHOUT going back to 1 first.
Practise entering the sequence from many different points — a visible number track or hundred square can mark where to begin.
Count on and across 100 to see the sequence continues (what comes after 100?), consistent with the 'to and across 100' standard.

Count backward from a given number: begin with short runs (e.g. 5 down to 0, then 15 down to 0) as scaffolds, then build up to 20 down to 0 without gaps, and on towards the full target of counting back from any given number up to 100 (e.g. 100 down to 90, 73 down to 60), including across decade boundaries. Use a number line or hundred square and, if helpful, a physical step-down for each number.
activities.intendedInsight: The number-word list should be accessible from any point and in both directions, not only as a single forward chant started at one.

activities.title: Daily rhythmic oral counting and take-turns buddy counting
feedback: If a learner says 'eleventeen' or maps a teen word to the wrong quantity, slow down and rehearse the teen stretch explicitly, distinguishing 'thirteen' from 'thirty' by sound.
Reinforce that chanting numbers with nothing attached is reciting the sequence, not counting objects — name which one you are doing each time.
Praise accurate turn-taking production, not just recognition of the right number when it is shown.
activities.rationale: Little-and-often oral practice builds the stable ordered list. The stable-order principle requires the words to be produced in the same order every time, and accurate object counting also needs the list to be at least as long as the set being counted. Take-turns oral dialogue is a legitimate oral-fluency drill here because the objective is verbal production; it does not make the ones-cycle pattern visible, so it complements rather than replaces hundred-square work.
sourceClaims: Stable-order principle: counting words must be said in a repeatable order, and the list must be at least as long as the set to be counted.
Year 1 verbatim: 'count to and across 100, forwards and backwards, beginning with 0 or 1, or from any given number'; guidance distinguishes counting as reciting from counting as enumerating objects.
learnerActions: Count aloud daily in short, rhythmic bursts — chants, songs or choral counting with the class or an adult.
Take turns with a partner (or a count-with-me buddy): you say one number, they say the next, alternating up the sequence.
When the buddy deliberately stumbles at a decade boundary ('…29… twenty-ten?'), catch and correct it.
Rehearse the irregular teens as a named stretch (eleven, twelve, thirteen…) and check you are not hearing 'thirteen' as 30.
activities.intendedInsight: The oral number sequence is built little and often, as sound and rhythm; taking turns and fixing a buddy's stumble makes the learner produce and monitor the sequence rather than just hear it.

activities.title: Fill the gap and fix the sequence (retrieval practice)
feedback: If an isolated number is missing or doubled, do NOT drill at speed — slow the pace and anchor on a hundred square, pointing to each; if the word string is broken, rebuild it gently rather than penalising.
Use gap-fill and ordering items as retrieval checks after oral and pattern work, not as the first teaching step.
activities.rationale: Short constructed-response items (fill the missing number, order steps, count back) give retrieval practice and surface specific breaks — but they check production of remembered numbers rather than teach the pattern, so they sit after the pattern and oral activities.
learnerActions: Fill in a missing number in a sequence (e.g. _, 29, _) and say what comes after 29 (30) and what comes just before 60 (59).
Put jumbled number cards back into order.
Count back a set number of steps from a given start.
Spot and fix a recite that has an omitted or doubled number (…14, 15, 17…).
activities.intendedInsight: Secure rote counting means you can enter, continue, reverse and repair the sequence — not only chant it from the start.

constraints: Reciting the number sequence is not the same as counting objects; keep both and name which is being done so chanting with nothing attached is not mistaken for enumeration.

Backward counting and starting mid-sequence are genuinely harder than forward-from-one and develop later; restarting at 1 or halting backward counting are developmental stages to practise, not errors to penalise.
Recognition or multiple-choice items check remembered numbers but do not elicit independent oral production of the sequence; include spoken recite tasks so the learner constructs the sequence aloud.
A hundred square makes the ones-cycle and decade structure visible, which supports prediction, but it does not by itself build oral fluency — pair it with daily spoken counting.
A static hundred square works as a reference chart (tap/point → number) but cannot itself drive a start-anywhere or backward count; the adult or learner must direct that movement.
Build the ordered list at least as long as needed before expecting accurate object counting over that range (you cannot count seven items if the names stop at six).
Distinguish 'thirteen' from 'thirty' and similar teen/decade pairs explicitly, as they are easily confused by sound.
The cited NC standard is 'to and across 100'; a little counting past 100 is within that standard, not off-objective, even though the short title says 'to 100'.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source's claim that a third dimension 'adds nothing' and that conversation is 'the one topic where dialogue-as-drill has real value' are catalog-fit opinions, not established facts; retained here only as the narrowly scoped observation that oral turn-taking suits an oral-production objective while a hundred square better shows pattern.
The NCETM hundred-square/early-number source is marked verified:false in the row; the pattern-visibility rationale drawing on it should be treated as unconfirmed.

The row is internally inconsistent on range: the parentTitle/description say 'to 100' while the quoted NC standard says 'count to and across 100'. Counting a little across 100 is therefore within the cited standard — a natural continuation showing the sequence does not stop at 100 — not an off-objective extension.

Whether the 69→70 (or 67→70) transition is literally a 'new row' depends on the hundred-square layout used (0–99 vs 1–100); the ones-cycle-and-increment-the-tens point holds regardless, so the inherited 'new row' wording is kept but should be matched to the actual square shown to the child.

topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} count in threes — 3, 6, 9, 12, 15 — far enough to reach 30 without losing track or needing to start over?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Ages 6–7 (Year 2). SKIP COUNTING in 3s, forwards and backwards from 0 — extends the equal-groups idea to a less familiar step size and prepares the 3× table. DfE explicitly links it to understanding 'a third'.
• Standards — UK (DfE): NC Year 2 verbatim 'count in steps of 2, 3, and 5 from 0, and in 10s from any number, forward and backward'; guidance: 'they count in multiples of 3 to support their later understanding of a third.'
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): counting in 3s is not a named CCSS skip-count (US names 5s/10s/100s at 2.NBT.2); it sits within multiplication foundations of Grade 2–3 (2.OA.4 arrays; 3.OA equal groups and 3× facts). The UK names 3s a year earlier than the US formalises the 3× table.
• Operational details: Because 3s don't align to hundred-square columns, the shaded pattern is a DIAGONAL stripe — use it to show 3s still form a regular pattern (defeats 'there's no pattern'). Count backwards from a multiple (30, 27, 24…) as well as forwards. Tie each step to one more group of three (arrays, repeated addition) and forward to the 3× table and to thirds.
• Checkpoint: Tier A counts in 3s from 0 to ~30 forwards. Tier B counts in 3s to at least 36 and backwards from 30. Tier C predicts the next multiple of 3 using the diagonal hundred-square pattern and links 3s to groups of three / the 3× table.
bestPractices: Show 3s as a DIAGONAL pattern on the hundred square so children see 3s are regular even though they don't line up in columns (counters the 'no pattern' feeling).
Insist on backward counting from a multiple (30, 27, 24…) — harder and needed for the full table.
Tie each step to one more group of three (arrays / repeated addition) and forward to the 3× table and 'a third' (the DfE link).
Play spot-the-multiple-of-3 on the hundred square, not only counting up from 0, so multiples are recognised anywhere.
keyRepresentations: Hundred square with multiples of 3 shaded (diagonal stripes).
Number line with equal 3-jumps.
Arrays / groups of three (bridge to the 3× table and thirds).
Backward-count track from 30.
commonMisconceptions: Feeling 3s have 'no pattern' because they don't form neat columns (they form diagonals).
Reciting 3s as isolated rote with no link to groups of three or the 3× table.
Being able to count forward but not backward in 3s.
Losing the step when crossing a decade (…18, 21…) — miscounting the +3 across the ten.

learn.summary: For ages 6–7 (UK Year 2): count in 3s forwards and backwards from 0, extending equal-groups thinking to a less familiar step size and seeding the 3× table and the idea of 'a third'. The central insight is that multiples of 3 still form a regular pattern — a diagonal pattern of repeating parallel lines on a hundred square — even though they do not line up in neat columns like 2s, 5s and 10s. Each step should be tied to one more group of three, and backward counting and mid-sequence continuation practised as skills in their own right.

activities.title: The diagonal reveal: shading 3s on a hundred square
feedback: If a child says 3s have 'no pattern', draw attention to the diagonal lines of shaded squares: the pattern is a slope rather than a column.
If the +3 step is lost crossing a decade — for example adding two and saying 20, or otherwise jumping the step and missing 21 as the next multiple — slow down at the ten and re-anchor: 18 + 3 = 21.
Optional interaction: let the child tap a shaded multiple to reveal its group of three, or watch cells recolour live as they step, so the pattern builds visibly.
activities.rationale: Showing 3s as a diagonal pattern on the hundred square makes their regularity visible and addresses the common sense that 3s are irregular because they don't form columns. Live shading and tap-to-reveal are optional ways to make the pattern concrete.
sourceClaims: Multiples of 3 form a diagonal pattern on the hundred square; showing the pattern counters the sense that 3s are irregular.
Year 2 verbatim: 'count in steps of 2, 3, and 5 from 0, and in 10s from any number, forward and backward'; guidance: 'they count in multiples of 3 to support their later understanding of a third.'
learnerActions: Step forward in 3s from 0 (3, 6, 9, 12…), shading or marking each multiple on a hundred square as you say it.
Notice that, unlike the vertical columns 5s and 10s make, the multiples of 3 march down the grid as repeating parallel diagonal lines (a diagonal pattern).
Use the diagonal pattern to predict the next multiple before you reach it, then check.
Play 'spot the multiple of 3' by pointing to multiples anywhere on the grid, not only counting up from 0.
Pay special attention to crossing each decade (…18, 21… and …27, 30…) so the +3 step is not lost across the ten.
activities.intendedInsight: Multiples of 3 are patterned, not random — the diagonal pattern lets you predict the next multiple and recognise multiples anywhere, countering the feeling that '3s have no pattern'.

activities.title: Number-line 3-jumps and groups of three
feedback: If a child recites 3s with no sense of grouping, lay out the arrays or counters so each jump matches a visible group of three.
Praise linking the jump count to the number of groups (e.g. 'five jumps, five threes, fifteen').
activities.rationale: Tying each skip-count step to an equal group bridges rote counting to multiplicative understanding and to the DfE link with thirds, preventing isolated rote recitation.
sourceClaims: Skip counting builds equal-groups understanding toward the multiplication tables (3.OA); arrays represent groups of three.
Year 2 verbatim: 'count in steps of 2, 3, and 5 from 0, and in 10s from any number, forward and backward'; guidance: 'they count in multiples of 3 to support their later understanding of a third.'
learnerActions: Make equal jumps of 3 along a number line, saying the multiple you land on each time.
For each jump, add one more group of three — show it with an array or counters (three counters per group) alongside the jump.
Connect 'four jumps of 3' to 'four groups of three' (four threes make 12) and to building up the 3× table.
Briefly link three equal groups making a whole to the idea of 'a third'.
activities.intendedInsight: Each step of 3 is one more group of three; stepping in 3s is the foundation of the 3× table and connects to thirds.

activities.title: Counting back and entering mid-sequence
feedback: If backward counting collapses or reverts to forward, slow to short runs with physical hops back along the line — treat it as a distinct skill.
If a child restarts at 3 to continue a mid-sequence, model 'the step is always +3, so add 3 to the last number you were given' and practise from several starting points; do not mark this wrong.

If each next multiple is reached by sub-counting ones under the breath (18… 19, 20, 21), do NOT drill for speed; make the step visible with number-line jumps of 3 and the diagonal pattern, and let fluency grow with exposure.
activities.rationale: Backward counting and mid-sequence entry are harder than the forward chant and are needed for the full table; sub-counting by ones is developmental and is addressed by making the +3 step visible rather than by speed drills.
sourceClaims: Year 2 verbatim: 'count in steps of 2, 3, and 5 from 0, and in 10s from any number, forward and backward'; guidance: 'they count in multiples of 3 to support their later understanding of a third.'
learnerActions: Count backwards in 3s from a multiple: 30, 27, 24… down to 0, using physical or drawn hops back along a number line.
Practise short backward runs (e.g. 12 → 0) as their own skill, not expecting it to come free with forward counting.
Continue a sequence from the middle: given 12, 15, 18, say the next number (and keep going) without restarting from 3.
Say the number just before a given multiple (e.g. what comes before 12 in the 3s).
activities.intendedInsight: Backward counting and continuing from any point are separate skills: the step is always +3 (or −3), so you can add or subtract 3 from the last number rather than restarting.

activities.title: Retrieval and oral fluency
feedback: Correct answers confirm the step; errors signal where to return to the hundred square or number line (e.g. decade crossings or backward runs).
Oral partner counting gives backward-count practice and fluency; pair it with the seen diagonal pattern on a hundred square so the visible pattern reinforces the underlying idea.
activities.rationale: Spaced retrieval and oral partner counting build fluency and expose children who only chant well-patterned sequences; these check and reinforce the understanding built visually rather than replacing it.
learnerActions: Answer quick questions: 'What is the next number in 3s?', fill a missing multiple in a sequence, put multiples of 3 in order, and count back in 3s.
With a partner, count aloud in 3s forwards and backwards, taking turns to say the next number.
Answer 'What's 3 more than 18?' (21) and 'What comes just before 12 in the 3s?' (9).
activities.intendedInsight: Fluency means stepping by three both ways and entering the sequence at any point, not only chanting up from 0.

constraints: Quick-recall questions and recognising/choosing the next multiple check and build fluency but do not by themselves elicit independent counting or the pattern insight; pair them with counting aloud and with the visible diagonal pattern.
Oral partner counting supports fluency and backward practice but does not show the diagonal pattern; combine it with a seen hundred square or number line.
Do not drill for speed when a child sub-counts intervals by ones — treat it as developmental and make the +3 step visible; fluency grows with exposure.
Treat backward counting and mid-sequence continuation as distinct skills to be practised, not as automatically following from forward counting.
The diagonal on the hundred square is a flat 2D pattern; it needs to be seen, but added depth/3D is not required to teach it.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two of the three cited sources were flagged unverified in the source row (the CCSS 3.OA reference and the NCETM diagonal-pattern guidance); the DfE Year 2 claim was marked verified. The diagonal-pattern claim underpins the headline activity but rests on an unverified citation.

On a standard 10-wide hundred square, multiples of 3 form several repeating parallel diagonal lines rather than literally one stripe; the wording was adjusted to 'diagonal pattern/lines' while keeping the original insight that 3s are regular.

The decade-crossing feedback in activity 1 was corrected so it no longer treats sub-counting-by-ones (which still lands on 21) as a decade-crossing error; that developmental pattern is handled in activity 3.

The original row rated a conversation/oral-count approach as only 'possible' and 3D as adding nothing; these were catalog fit rankings. They are reframed here as affordances/limits (oral counting aids fluency but lacks the visible pattern; depth is not needed) rather than universal claims that one medium alone can teach the concept.

The pedagogy section's Tier A/B/C checkpoint descriptions were not carried verbatim into the learner-facing activities; they overlap with the assess gap/partial/full response levels reflected across activities.

topic.name: Counting forwards and backwards (age 6+)
topic.description: Count forwards and backwards in tens from any number (not just multiples of 10)
evidence: Count 7, 17, 27, 37 … from a non-multiple starting point
Count backwards in tens from 83
Explain the pattern of adding/subtracting 10
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} starts at 37 and you ask them to count up in tens, can they say 37, 47, 57, 67 — crossing over into the next hundred without getting stuck?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Ages 6–7 (Year 2). COUNTING IN TENS FROM ANY NUMBER (not just multiples of 10) — e.g. 7, 17, 27, 37… A place-value insight: adding/subtracting 10 changes only the TENS digit; the ones digit stays the same. The foundation for mental +10/−10 and column place value.
• Standards — UK (DfE): NC Year 2 'count … in 10s from any number, forward and backward'; Year 3 'find 10 or 100 more or less than a given number'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 1.NBT.5 'Given a two-digit number, mentally find 10 more or 10 less than the number, without having to count'; extends to 2.NBT.8. Directly parallel to the UK statement.
• Operational details: Teach on the HUNDRED SQUARE as a VERTICAL move — straight DOWN a column = +10, straight UP = −10 — so the child SEES the tens digit tick while the ones digit is fixed; contrast with counting in ones (a horizontal move). Use base-ten blocks (add a ten-rod; ones untouched) for the concrete why. Say the rule aloud: 'the ones stay the same'. Practise forwards and backwards from non-multiples (83, 73, 63…).
• Checkpoint: Tier A counts in 10s from a non-multiple forward (4, 14, 24…). Tier B counts in 10s forward and backward from any two-digit number and states that the tens digit changes. Tier C explains WHY only the tens digit changes (one more ten, ones unchanged) and does it mentally.
bestPractices: Teach it as a VERTICAL move on the hundred square (down = +10, up = −10) so the tens-digit change and the fixed ones-digit are seen.
Use base-ten blocks: add one ten-rod while the ones pile is untouched — the concrete 'why' behind the digit rule.
Say the rule aloud — 'the ones stay the same, the tens go up by one' — and test it from many non-multiple starts.
Practise backward (−10) from any number; connect to mental 10-more / 10-less.
keyRepresentations: Hundred square (vertical move = ±10; ones digit fixed down a column).
Base-ten blocks / Dienes (add or remove a ten-rod).
Place-value chart (tens column changes, ones column unchanged).
Number line with 10-jumps from a non-round start.
commonMisconceptions: Changing the ones digit too (e.g. 27 → 38) — not isolating the +10 to the tens.
Only able to add 10 to multiples of 10 (can't start from 7 or 23).
Treating +10 as 'just add a 0' — which fails for non-round numbers (27 ≠ 270).
Losing the column on the hundred square (drifting sideways instead of straight down).

learn.summary: For ages 6–7 (Year 2): counting in tens from ANY number, not just multiples of ten (e.g. 7, 17, 27, 37…). The core place-value insight is that adding or subtracting 10 keeps the ones digit the same while the tens digit changes by one — and at a hundred boundary such as 96 → 106 the tens roll from 9 to 0 and a new hundred appears (backwards, 106 → 96, they roll from 0 to 9), while the ones digit still does not move. This is the foundation for mental +10/−10 and later column place value. It is best made visible as a vertical move on a hundred square (on a standard square numbered from 1 at the top, straight down = +10 and straight up = −10; check the direction on squares numbered from the bottom), with concrete support from base-ten blocks (add/remove a ten-rod, ones untouched). Practise forwards and backwards from non-multiples and say the rule aloud.

activities.title: Down a column, ones frozen — the +10/−10 move on the hundred square
feedback: If a learner recites decade names (7 → 10, 20, 30) and drops the 7: on the hundred square move straight DOWN the column from 7 to show 7, 17, 27 keep the ones digit; name aloud what stays (the 7) and what changes (the tens).

If the ones digit drifts (7, 17, 28, 38): do NOT reteach counting — highlight that the ones column stays the same, using place-value arrow cards or adding one ten-rod each time so the +10-only structure is felt.

If a learner stalls at the hundred boundary (fine to 97, then stuck or says 100, 110): extend the square past 100 and rehearse just the 97 → 107 → 117 bridge, pointing out the ones digit (7) still stays while the tens roll from 9 to 0 and a new hundred appears. Saying 100 means the ones digit has changed, so revisit what stays the same and give more practice crossing 100.

If a learner says +10 means 'add a 0' (27 → 270): compare 27+10 on the grid with the actual answer 37. Show that adding a 0 multiplies by ten, so it never gives +10, even for round numbers (20 with a 0 added is 200, but 20+10 = 30).
activities.rationale: A vertical hop on the hundred square keeps all numbers in a column sharing the same ones digit, so the fixed ones and ticking tens are seen directly. An optional linked panel updating the numeral — ones digit staying lit while the tens change — and a synchronised base-ten rod can make the mechanism concrete, though a printed hundred square with a counter supports the same move.
sourceClaims: Counting in tens from any number is a place-value move best shown as a vertical move on the hundred square (tens change, ones fixed).
learnerActions: Start on a non-multiple, e.g. 27, on a hundred square.
Make a +10 move by dropping straight DOWN one row: 27 → 37 → 47 → 57, saying each number aloud.
Each step of this 27 → 57 run, point to the ones digit (the 7) and say 'the ones stay the same'; point to the tens digit and say 'the tens go up by one' (true while you stay inside a hundred).
Reverse it: make −10 moves by going straight UP one row: 83 → 73 → 63 → 53, saying what stays (the ones) and what changes (the tens).
Watch for drifting sideways — keep the move strictly vertical so you stay in the same ones-digit column.
activities.intendedInsight: Adding or subtracting ten never touches the ones digit; it is the same single downward (or upward) step on the hundred square whatever number you start from. '+10' is not 'add a zero' — it is 'one row down'.

activities.title: Concrete why: add a ten-rod with base-ten blocks
feedback: If a learner changes the ones to make +10, point out the ones pile should not have been touched and rebuild it.
Connect the blocks back to the digits: the number of ten-rods is the tens digit, the ones pile is the ones digit.
activities.rationale: Manipulating ten-rods gives a physical cause for the digit rule, complementing the grid picture with hands-on structure.
learnerActions: Build a two-digit number with base-ten blocks, e.g. 23 as two ten-rods and three ones.
To add 10, bring in ONE more ten-rod and leave the ones pile untouched; read the new number (33).
To subtract 10, take one ten-rod away and leave the ones pile untouched; read the new number.
Say the rule as you go: 'one more ten, the ones don't change'.
Link each action to its numeral and, if available, to the hundred-square move.
activities.intendedInsight: Physically, +10 is just one extra ten-rod; the ones stay as they are. This is the concrete reason the ones digit never changes.

activities.title: Say-it and spot-the-slip practice
feedback: If a learner finds 10 more only by counting on in ones, encourage the direct 'one row down' move instead.
When a learner spots the wrong digit, ask them to correct it and state the rule.
Recognising a wrong sequence is a check; it does not by itself show the learner can produce a correct one, so also ask the learner to generate their own sequences aloud.
activities.rationale: Mixed forward/backward retrieval and error-spotting consolidate the rule and surface misconceptions. This reinforces, rather than replaces, the grid and blocks work where the insight is first seen.
learnerActions: Answer quick questions: 'What is 10 more than 47?' and 'What is 10 less than 47?'
Fill in a tens sequence from a non-multiple, e.g. 4, 14, __, __, 44.
Look at a wrong sequence (e.g. 7, 17, 28, 38) and say which digit changed that shouldn't have.
Count aloud forwards from a non-multiple and backwards from a two-digit number, stating each step is +10 or −10.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent +10/−10 from any starting number, with the ability to notice when the ones digit has wrongly moved.

activities.title: Explain the pattern out loud
feedback: Accept explanations like 'you add one more ten, so the ones don't move'.
For ten more than 96, let the learner use the extended grid to see 96 → 106: point out that the ones digit (6) still does not move, while the tens roll from 9 to 0 and a new hundred appears.
activities.rationale: Explaining the structure distinguishes a child who understands tens-and-ones from one who is reciting a memorised sequence.
learnerActions: Count in tens from a non-multiple, then answer: 'What stays the same each time, and what changes?'
Answer in your own words why the ones digit stays the same each time and what happens to the tens.
Try harder prompts: ten less than 43 (33); ten more than 96 (106, crossing 100).
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to articulate that each step adds or removes one ten — so the ones digit always stays the same while the tens digit changes by one, rolling over into a new hundred at a boundary like 96 → 106 where the ones (6) still does not move — shows place-value reasoning rather than just the chant.

constraints: Always practise from NON-multiples (7, 23, 83…), not just 10, 20, 30 — multiples can be done by chanting decade names without the place-value insight.
Include backward (−10) as well as forward counting; backward from a two-digit number additionally tests subtraction of ten.

State the robust invariant to children: the ones digit always stays the same. The tens digit normally goes up (or down) by one, but at a hundred boundary it rolls over: forwards (96 → 106) it goes from 9 to 0 and a new hundred appears; backwards (106 → 96) it goes from 0 to 9 and the hundred goes. The ones digit is unchanged either way.
A hundred-square counter or screen model shows the move but is a representation; pair it with base-ten blocks for the concrete 'why' when a learner only mimics the grid.
Error-spotting and 'which digit is wrong' tasks check recognition; also require the learner to produce sequences and explanations independently.
Do not teach '+10 means add a 0' — adding a 0 multiplies by ten, so it never gives +10 (27+10 = 37, not 270; 20+10 = 30, not 200).
Keep the move strictly vertical on the hundred square; drifting sideways reverts to counting in ones.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; the sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original flagged a 3D representation as 'adding nothing'; this universal comparative claim has been dropped. A planar hundred square is well suited here, but no comparative-efficacy claim against other media is asserted.

The original rated an oral back-and-forth as only 'possible' because the ones-fixed insight is 'best seen on the grid'. Spoken practice is retained as useful consolidation; the categorical claim that the grid is uniquely able to teach the insight is softened to a scoped affordance (the grid makes the fixed ones/ticking tens visible).

The original summary and probe phrase the rule as '+10/−10 changes only the tens digit'. This holds within a hundred but not across a hundred boundary (96+10=106: the ones digit 6 is unchanged, but the tens roll 9→0 and a new hundred appears). Learner-facing text foregrounds the always-true invariant — the ones digit stays fixed — while describing the tens roll-over; the original simplification is noted here only.

The 'number line with 10-jumps from a non-round start' listed in the source representations is not implemented as a dedicated activity; it is compatible but was not carried into the learner-facing tasks.

Arithmetic checked: 27+10=37,47,57; 83−10=73,63,53; 23+10=33; 96+10=106; 97+10=107, 107+10=117; 43−10=33; 4,14,24,34,44 is consistent. Decade-snapping error (7→10,20,30) and ones-drift (7,17,28,38) are preserved as learner errors to diagnose, not as instructions to follow.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Counting Within 1,000
topic.description: Count within 1000, including skip-counting by 5s, 10s, and 100s
evidence: Count forwards and backwards within 1000 from any starting number
Skip-count by 5s from any multiple of 5 to 1000
Skip-count by 100s from any number (e.g. 150, 250, 350 …)
topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} count confidently up to 1000 — and if you ask them to count by hundreds from 200, or by tens from 650, can they do it without losing their place?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 7–8 (UK Y2→Y3, US Grade 2). Counting within 1,000, including skip-counting by 5s, 10s and 100s and understanding what changes as you cross into the hundreds.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y2 'count in steps of 2, 3, and 5 from 0, and in tens from any number' and use of <, >, =; Y3 'count from 0 in multiples of 4, 8, 50 and 100' and 'find 10 or 100 more or less than a given number', with fluent order and place value to 1,000.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 2.NBT.2 'Count within 1000; skip-count by 5s, 10s, and 100s'; 2.NBT.8 'mentally add/subtract 10 or 100 to a given number 100–900'.
• Operational details: the leap from within-100 to within-1000 is a PLACE-VALUE leap, not just a longer chant — +10 rolls the tens digit, +100 rolls the hundreds digit, and the child must see WHICH digit changes. Skip from non-round starts (e.g. 5s from 315, 100s from 240). The reliable stall is crossing hundred boundaries (190→200, 995→1000) where a digit carries.
• Checkpoint: skip-count aloud and predict the crossing. Tier A (7): count on in 10s and 100s from a round number within 1000 with a hundred-square/number-line prop. Tier B (7–8): skip-count by 5s/10s/100s from any start and state 10-more/100-more without counting. Tier C (8): cross 190→200 and 970→1000 explaining which digit rolls and why.
bestPractices: Frame within-1000 counting as PLACE VALUE in motion: use base-ten materials (hundreds flats, tens rods, unit cubes) so +10 physically adds a rod and +100 adds a flat — the child sees the digit that changes rather than reciting.

Make crossing a hundred boundary the explicit teaching event: pause at 190, ask 'what comes next in 10s?', and show the ten tens rods trading for one hundred flat so the roll from 190→200 is felt, not mysterious.
Skip-count from non-round and 'ragged' starts (5s from 315, 10s from 268, 100s from 240) so the pattern is a rule about which digit moves, not a memorised round-number chant.

Sync three representations of the same skip count — hundred/thousand grid highlights, equal jumps on a number line, and equal groups of counters — so 100s counting is seen as repeated equal groups (the multiplication/place-value bridge).
Separate '10 more' from 'count on ten by ones': ask for 10-more and 100-more instantly and check the child is rolling a digit, not counting 1,2,3… to prove the place-value idea has landed.
keyRepresentations: Scalable number line marked to 1,000 with equal jumps (jumps of 10 and of 100) to show constant step size and boundary crossings
Thousand grid / linked hundred squares where each skip count lights a column or diagonal, exposing the 5s, 10s and 100s patterns
Base-ten blocks (unit cubes, tens rods, hundreds flats) with regrouping — ten rods trade for one flat at the hundred boundary
Place-value columns (H T U) with digit-rollers so a step by 10 or 100 visibly advances one column and carries into the next
commonMisconceptions: Hundred-boundary stall — reaching 190 the child says '191, 192…' or '100-ten', not knowing 200 comes next; the decade/hundred bridge is the classic breakdown point.
'+10 means add a zero' / '+100 means add two zeros' — over-generalised from round numbers, so 268+10 becomes 2680 or 26810.
Treating the count as a longer rote chant and losing track of which digit changes, so skip-counting from a non-round start collapses.
Confusing tens and hundreds steps (counting 240, 250, 260 when asked to skip in 100s) because the difference between which column moves is not yet secure.
Losing the ones digit when skip-counting by 10s or 100s from a ragged start (315→320 instead of 325) because the child re-rounds to a decade.

learn.summary: For ages 7–8 (UK Y2→Y3, US Grade 2), skip-counting within 1,000 by 5s, 10s and 100s is a place-value event, not a longer chant: the learner must see WHICH digit rolls when adding 5, 10 or 100, and why a carry happens when crossing a hundred (190→200) or thousand (995→1000) boundary. Core activities drive a live place-value counter from round and ragged starts, with static reference and checking tasks as supports. Non-round starts (5s from 315, 100s from 150/240, 10s from 268) are emphasised so the learner holds the other digits fixed rather than re-rounding to a decade.

activities.title: Place-value skip-count playground (drive the carry)
feedback: If the learner predicts '2680' for 268+10 (the 'add a zero' error), pause the counter and show only the tens column advancing 6→7 to give 278; name that +10 moves one column, it does not append a digit.
If a ragged start collapses to a decade when counting on in 10s (315→320 instead of the correct 325), highlight the fixed ones digit (5) and replay the jump so the learner sees the ones stay put.
At the boundary, if the learner hesitates, show the ten tens-rods snapping into one hundred-flat so the carry is seen rather than recited.

When a '10 more' answer is produced instantly and correctly, confirm by rolling the tens digit (plus the regrouped next digit if a boundary is crossed), reinforcing that this is a place-value move, not counting on by ones.
activities.rationale: The classic stall is at hundred/thousand boundaries and from non-round starts; a learner-driven counter that synchronises grid, number line and place-value columns lets the child predict then see the exact digit that rolls, targeting the 'add a zero' and re-rounding misconceptions directly.
sourceClaims: 2.NBT.2: Count within 1000; skip-count by 5s, 10s, and 100s. 2.NBT.8: mentally add 10 or 100 to, and subtract 10 or 100 from, a given number 100–900.
Skip counting is a bridge to multiplicative reasoning and place value, not rote chanting; regrouping at ten/hundred boundaries is a core mastery checkpoint.
learnerActions: Set a start number — round (e.g. 240) or ragged (e.g. 315, 268) — and choose a step of +5, +10 or +100.
Before tapping, predict aloud the next number and say which digit you think will change.

Tap the step and watch three linked views move together: a thousand grid lights the landed number, a number line draws one equal jump, and place-value columns (H-T-U, with a Th column that appears when you reach 1000) roll the digit or digits that change.
Stop deliberately at 190 and predict 'what comes next in 10s?', then tap +10 and watch ten tens-rods trade for one hundred-flat while the hundreds digit rolls 1→2 and the tens resets to 0.
Repeat the boundary move by counting in 5s up to 995→1000 and describe, in your own words, which columns carried.

Switch to a '10 more / 100 more instantly' challenge: state the answer without counting on by ones, then tap to check which digit rolled (just one digit unless the step crosses a hundred or thousand boundary, e.g. 195 → 205).
activities.intendedInsight: Adding 10 rolls the tens digit and adding 100 rolls the hundreds digit; if no boundary is crossed, the other digits stay the same. When a hundred/thousand boundary is crossed (e.g. 190 → 200), the next place up also changes because of regrouping (ten of one place trading for one of the next), not a mysterious jump.

activities.title: Hands-on regrouping with base-ten materials
feedback: If the learner counts 150, 250, 350 but drops the 50 to say 100, 200, 300, point to the five tens rods still sitting on the mat and ask what should have stayed the same.
If the learner recites a number but adds the wrong piece, map the spoken digit to the matching column of blocks before continuing.
activities.rationale: Base-ten materials make +10/+100 a concrete regrouping action, so the child can see which digit changes rather than reciting a longer chant; this grounds the live on-screen counter.
sourceClaims: Skip counting is a bridge to multiplicative reasoning and place value, not rote chanting; regrouping at ten/hundred boundaries is a core mastery checkpoint.
learnerActions: Build a start number with hundreds flats, tens rods and unit cubes (e.g. 190 as one flat and nine rods).
To add 10, physically add one tens rod; to add 100, add one hundreds flat — and say which digit changed.
At 190, add the tenth rod, then trade ten rods for one hundreds flat to make 200, and say 'the tens rolled to 0 and the hundreds went up by one'.
Skip-count by 100s from 150 using flats, keeping the five tens and nothing in the ones fixed, to reach 250, 350 … 950.
activities.intendedInsight: Adding 10 or 100 physically adds a rod or a flat, and crossing a boundary is the concrete act of trading ten rods for one flat — making the digit that changes something the learner can handle and see, not just recite.

activities.title: Annotated thousand-square and place-value reference
feedback: If the learner names the wrong column for a step, point back to the lit pattern and the H-T-U labels so the step size maps to a single column.
Use the boundary flap as a reminder that the join between 190 and 200 is a trade, to be practised live with the counter or blocks.
activities.rationale: A static annotated reference is a strong support for recognising patterns and naming columns, but recognition alone does not enact the carry or recompute from a ragged start, so it accompanies rather than replaces the manipulable counter.
learnerActions: Study a thousand grid / linked hundred squares where a 10s count lights one column, a 5s count lights two columns, and a 100s count lights the same position in each hundred square, and name the pattern you see.
Tap a highlighted 100s column to reveal the note 'each step adds one hundred — the hundreds digit changes', and name the H, T, U columns.
Open the flap at the 190→200 join to read how ten tens trade for one hundred.
activities.intendedInsight: The 5s/10s/100s patterns fall in predictable places (columns for 5s and 10s, the same position in each hundred square for 100s), and naming the place-value columns helps the learner say which digit each step advances.

activities.title: Checking and diagnostic skip-count tasks
feedback: Expected: 150, 250 … 950; 480, 485 … 520 crossing 500 correctly; 1000, 990, 980 …; and 620, 720, 820, 920, 1020 crossing the thousand boundary cleanly. (985, __, 1005 fills to 995.)
'10 more than 268' = 278; if a learner offers 2680, that is the 'add a zero' error — show the tens digit rolling 6→7 instead. ('100 more than 613' = 713.)
If the learner snaps 100s-from-150 to 100, 200, 300, name the dropped 50 and re-run keeping tens and ones fixed.

If an error appears precisely at 495→500 or at 1000 while mid-run counting is fine, treat it as a boundary-bridge gap: rehearse just 490, 495, 500, 505 and 980, 990, 1000, 1010 on a number line, naming the regrouping — do not re-drill the whole sequence.
If backward counting breaks only at boundaries, practise short backward runs across each boundary as its own skill; do not assume backward fluency arrives with forward.
activities.rationale: Boundary-crossing and ragged-start items probe the key misconceptions crisply and separate secure three-digit place value from a learner who snaps to pure multiples or re-rounds; placed after the constructive activities they primarily verify the insight, while their feedback can reteach when an error appears.
sourceClaims: 2.NBT.2: Count within 1000; skip-count by 5s, 10s, and 100s. 2.NBT.8: mentally add 10 or 100 to, and subtract 10 or 100 from, a given number 100–900.
Skip counting is a bridge to multiplicative reasoning and place value, not rote chanting; regrouping at ten/hundred boundaries is a core mastery checkpoint.
learnerActions: Order a set of 100s cards from 240 and fill blanks in sequences that cross a boundary, e.g. 985, __, 1005.
Answer '100 more than 613' and '10 more than 268', writing the single digit that changed.
Count on in 100s from 150 up to 950; count in 5s from 480 up to 520; count back in 10s from 1000; count on in 100s from 620 and say what happens when the count passes 1000 (920 → 1020).
Explain for each: which digit changed and which stayed the same.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluency means changing only the relevant place and crossing hundred and thousand boundaries cleanly, from non-round starts and in both directions.

activities.title: Count-with-me partner rehearsal (spoken practice)
feedback: If the learner supplies a wrong boundary number, pause and return to a number line or blocks to show the regrouping before resuming the count.
Reward a correct boundary supply by having the learner name the digit that changed.
activities.rationale: Spoken turn-taking rehearses the sequence orally and prompts boundary crossings; it adds oral practice alongside the visual/place-value work rather than replacing the manipulable or concrete activities.
learnerActions: Take turns skip-counting aloud with a counting buddy, alternating each number in a 10s or 100s run.
When the buddy hesitates at 190 in a 10s run, supply the next number (200) and say which digits rolled.
Say each number clearly and, at boundaries, state what carried before moving on.
activities.intendedInsight: Rehearsing the count aloud, especially at the deliberate hesitation at a boundary, builds oral fluency and the habit of naming the carry.

constraints: The annotated thousand-square and place-value reference is a scaffold: it shows patterns and names columns but does not itself enact the carry or recompute from a ragged start, so pair it with a manipulable counter or base-ten materials.

Checking/diagnostic tasks are primarily for verifying the pattern and catching misconceptions; their feedback can also prompt reteaching, but they are best placed after the constructive activities rather than being the sole means of building the place-value insight.
Spoken partner practice rehearses the sequence orally but does not by itself make the digit-rolling visible; keep it alongside visual/concrete work.

Base-ten cutouts and rods are physical approximations of the ideal place-value idea: use the trade of ten rods for one flat to represent regrouping, and connect the concrete piece to the spoken digit and the written column.
Practise backward counting across boundaries as its own skill rather than assuming it transfers automatically from forward fluency.
When crossing a boundary during a ragged-start count, keep the ones/tens that should stay fixed in view so the learner does not re-round to a decade.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched and the activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
