pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 7–8 (UK Y3, US Grade 2–3). Skip counting in 4s, 8s, 50s and 100s — extending equal-step counting into the multiplication-facts that underpin the times tables.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y3 'count from 0 in multiples of 4, 8, 50 and 100'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 2.NBT.2 'skip-count by 5s, 10s, and 100s'; 3.OA.7 recall of products (the 4s and 8s underpin the ×4 and ×8 tables); 3.NBT.3 multiply one-digit by multiples of 10.
• Operational details: teach 4s and 8s through the DOUBLING CHAIN — 2s doubled give 4s, 4s doubled give 8s (each 8-step is two 4-steps is four 2-steps). 50s are half-hundreds/money (two 50s make 100) and 100s extend the place-value step. Counting in 4s and 8s is explicitly the equal-groups on-ramp to the 4 and 8 times tables.
• Checkpoint: skip-count fluently and connect to equal groups. Tier A (7): count in 4s and 100s from 0 with a number-line/hundred-square prop. Tier B (7–8): count in 4s, 8s, 50s, 100s from 0 and state the matching equal-groups fact (three 4s = 12). Tier C (8): explain 8s as doubled 4s and 4s as doubled 2s, and count 50s to 500 linking two 50s = 100.
bestPractices: Build 4s and 8s from the DOUBLING relationship rather than as separate chants: stack a 2s number line, a 4s line and an 8s line so the child sees each 4-jump spans two 2-jumps and each 8-jump spans two 4-jumps.

Tie every skip count to equal groups and the array — counting 4, 8, 12, 16 is one group, two groups, three groups of four — so skip counting is experienced as repeated addition and the direct route into the ×4 and ×8 tables.
Anchor 50s in money and half-hundreds: two 50p coins make £1, two 50s make 100, so counting 50, 100, 150 is felt as pairing up to hundreds rather than a new memorised list.
Use the hundred square to expose the visual pattern of each count (the 4s and 8s make regular diagonal/column patterns; 50s and 100s march down rows) so the pattern is seen, not just heard.

Rehearse forwards and backwards and from non-zero starts once the forward count is secure, and connect back to previously mastered 2s/5s/10s so the new counts join a coherent web rather than standing alone.
keyRepresentations: Stacked/aligned number lines (2s, 4s, 8s) showing the doubling of jump size
Equal groups and arrays (groups of 4, groups of 8) linking the count to repeated addition and multiplication
Hundred square with each multiple shaded to reveal the pattern (4s, 8s columns/diagonals; 50s and 100s down the rows)
Coins and a money line (50p, £1) anchoring the 50s count in half-hundreds
commonMisconceptions: Treating 4s and 8s as unrelated rote lists and never noticing 8s are doubled 4s — so a slip in one count cannot be repaired from the other.
Adding the wrong step (drifting into 2s when counting 4s, or 5s when counting 50s) because the step size isn't held steady.
Miscounting 50s as 'fifties are like fives with a zero' and producing 50, 100, 150, 250 — losing a step or mis-pairing to hundreds.
Not connecting the skip count to groups, so the child can chant 4, 8, 12 but cannot say how many groups of four make 12 — the count stays verbal and never becomes multiplicative.
Boundary slips crossing hundreds while counting in 50s or 100s (150→200, 950→1000) when the hundreds digit must roll.

learn.summary: For ages 7–8 (UK Y3, US Grade 2–3): counting from 0 in multiples of 4, 8, 50 and 100, built on the doubling chain (2s doubled are 4s, 4s doubled are 8s) and tied explicitly to equal groups so skip counting becomes the on-ramp to the ×4 and ×8 tables. 50s are anchored in money/half-hundreds (two 50s make 100). The central insight to teach is the relationship between step sizes — that each 8-jump spans two 4-jumps spans four 2-jumps — and the connection between a verbal count and 'how many groups'.

activities.title: The doubling chain: stacked number lines for 2s, 4s and 8s
feedback: If a learner sub-counts (audibly counting 4-by-4 or one-by-one to reach the next 8), do not drill for speed. Point to the known 4s fact and prompt 'double it' — fluency grows through repeated jumps on the number line, not pressure.
If a learner treats 4s and 8s as unrelated, write out the 4s from 0 and ring every second number (0, 8, 16…) to reveal the 8s: 'the 8s take a jump twice as big.'
When a learner lands correctly, ask them to show which smaller jumps live inside the big jump, so the doubling is explained, not just recited.
activities.rationale: The target relationship is between step sizes, which becomes visible when the counts are laid against each other and the jumps aligned. Building 4s and 8s from doubling rather than as separate chants gives learners a repair strategy and links directly to the ×4 and ×8 tables. Optional interactive versions (buttons that advance each line, with smaller jumps ghosting in beneath each larger step) may make the nesting more manipulable; a paper version with three aligned strips achieves the same alignment.
sourceClaims: Skip counting in 4s and 8s is developed via the doubling relationship and as the equal-groups route into multiplication tables.
learnerActions: Lay out (or display) three aligned number lines starting at 0: one marked in 2s, one in 4s, one in 8s, with the same spacing so matching numbers sit directly above one another.
Step along the 8s line one jump at a time. For each 8-jump, mark the two 4-jumps directly beneath it, and the four 2-jumps beneath those.
Say aloud as you go: 'one jump of 8 is the same distance as two jumps of 4, which is four jumps of 2.'
Count the 4s aloud (0, 4, 8, 12, 16…) and ring every other number starting from 0 — notice the circled numbers are exactly the 8s count (0, 8, 16…).
Count backwards in 8s from 96, checking each step against the 4s line.
Repeat from a non-zero start once the forward count is secure (e.g. count on in 4s from 24).
Link the new counts back to the 2s, 5s and 10s you already know, so 4s/8s/50s/100s join a coherent web rather than standing alone.
activities.intendedInsight: 8s are doubled 4s and 4s are doubled 2s; a slip in one count can be repaired using the other, because the step sizes nest inside each other.

activities.title: From skip count to equal groups and arrays
feedback: If a learner can chant '4, 8, 12' but cannot say how many groups of four make 12, rebuild with physical groups so each number names one more group.
If a learner answers 'how many fours in 20' by guessing, have them step the number line and tally the jumps.
Confirm success when the learner moves fluently between the count, the groups and the product.
activities.rationale: Tying every skip count to equal groups and the array makes the count multiplicative rather than purely verbal, and matching items test the count-to-groups connection directly. This is the bridge from counting to table recall.
sourceClaims: 2.NBT.2 skip-count by 5s, 10s and 100s; 3.OA.7 fluently multiply and recall products — counting in 4s and 8s underpins the ×4 and ×8 tables.
Skip counting in 4s and 8s is developed via the doubling relationship and as the equal-groups route into multiplication tables.
learnerActions: Build groups of four with counters: one group, two groups, three groups, saying the running total (4, 8, 12) and the matching fact ('three fours = 12').
Arrange the same counters into an array (rows of four) so each skip-count step adds one row.
Match skip-count totals to equal-groups statements, e.g. pair 'three groups of 8' with 24, 'five fours' with 20.
Answer group-count challenges in both directions: 'How many fours in 20?' (five) and 'What is four groups of eight?' (32).
Repeat the build for groups of eight, noticing each group of eight is two groups of four.
activities.intendedInsight: A skip count is repeated addition of equal groups; knowing the count lets you say how many groups make a total, which is exactly the multiplication fact.

activities.title: Counting in 50s and 100s with money and the hundred square
feedback: If a learner says 50, 100, 150, 250 (losing a step), do not reteach the whole sequence — rehearse the specific boundary bridge (…, 150, 200) with coins or a number line.
If a learner loses place crossing a hundred, slow down at the boundary and name the rolling hundreds digit aloud.

If a learner uses '50s are like 5s with a zero', accept it as a valid pattern (each 50s number is ten times the matching 5s number), and also build meaning by pairing coins to hundreds so they can explain why 150 + 50 = 200.
activities.rationale: Anchoring 50s in money and half-hundreds makes the count felt as pairing to hundreds rather than a new memorised list, and the hundred square and number line expose the visual pattern so it is seen, not only heard. Targeting boundary crossings addresses a common place-value slip. No cited source directly supports this money-anchoring approach, so it is offered as a research-informed proposal.
learnerActions: Pair up 50p coins (or £50 notes) to make pounds/hundreds: two 50s make 100, so count 50, 100, 150, 200… pairing as you go.
Count on in 50s from 0 to 1000, deliberately slowing at each hundred boundary (…, 450, 500, 550; …, 950, 1000) and checking the hundreds digit rolls correctly.

On a 1–100 hundred square, shade the 4s and 8s to see their column/diagonal patterns; then on a number line or track to 1000, mark the 50s and 100s to see them step evenly, with 50s landing twice as often as 100s.
Count in 100s from 0 to 1000 and compare with the 50s on the same number line.
State explicitly: 'how many 50s make 1000?' and check by pairing (two 50s = 100, so twenty 50s = 1000).
activities.intendedInsight: Counting in 50s can be understood as pairing up to hundreds (two 50s make 100); it also matches the 5s count with each number ten times bigger (5, 10, 15 → 50, 100, 150), but the pairing view carries the meaning. Boundary crossings require the hundreds digit to roll, and shading/marking makes each count's pattern visible.

activities.title: Oral fluency and self-check with a counting partner
feedback: If totals disagree between the 8s and 'two lots of 4s' check, find the step where they diverge and re-jump it.
Praise self-correction that uses the 4s to repair the 8s rather than restarting.
activities.rationale: Spoken rehearsal with responsive prompting may support oral fluency and keeps the doubling link active; it is intended to complement the visual/structural work rather than replace it, and is best used once the structure is understood rather than as the first route in. Its effectiveness relative to the manipulative is untested.
sourceClaims: Skip counting in 4s and 8s is developed via the doubling relationship and as the equal-groups route into multiplication tables.
learnerActions: Count in 8s aloud with a partner, taking turns on each step.
Check an 8s count against the 4s count, confirming that each 8s step equals two 4s steps (e.g. two jumps of 4 reach 8, four jumps of 4 reach 16).
Have the partner pose doubling prompts: 'If four fours are 16, what are four eights?'
Count forwards and backwards from non-zero starts to build flexibility, and relate the counts to the already-known 2s, 5s and 10s.
activities.intendedInsight: Oral rehearsal and self-checking against a related count build fluency and reinforce that the 4s and 8s support each other.

constraints: Counting in 4s and 8s is best built from the doubling relationship, not taught as separate rote chants, so learners can repair one count from the other.
Every skip count should be tied to equal groups/arrays so the count becomes multiplicative, not merely verbal.
Do not drill for speed when a learner is sub-counting; connect to the known related count and let fluency grow through repeated jumps and retrieval.

Sequence, fill-in-the-blank and matching exercises can check these counts but do not by themselves build the doubling structure — use them to check mastery after the relationship has been taught; a sort/match verifies classification without eliciting an explanation of why 8s are doubled 4s.

A pre-shaded pattern reference (static or tap-to-reveal) supports pattern spotting and the equal-groups link but does not let the learner drive the count or see the doubling animate; treat it as a reference, not the primary build.

Interactive overlays (advancing lines, ghosted smaller jumps, live shading) and physical coins are optional concrete aids to make the mechanism visible; they are means, not required mechanisms — aligned paper strips and real coins work too.
A standard 1–100 hundred square displays the 4s/8s patterns; use a number line or track for 50s and 100s up to 1000.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources have not been re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of the counts: 4s from 0 to 48 (0,4,8,12,16,20,24,28,32,36,40,44,48), 8s from 0 to 96 (0,8,…,96), and 50s to 1000 (twenty steps of 50) are all arithmetically consistent. 'Every second multiple of 4, counting from 0, is a multiple of 8' is correct (0,8,16… are the even-indexed 4s). Equal-groups facts used are correct: three fours = 12, five fours = 20, three eights = 24, four eights = 32, twenty fifties = 1000.
The source's erroneous example sequence '50, 100, 150, 250' (used to illustrate a learner error) is preserved only as a misconception to correct, never presented as a valid count.

Two of three cited sources are marked verified:false in the source row (the CCSS-M and NCETM claims); treat their specific wordings as unconfirmed, and the doubling/equal-groups pedagogy as a recommended rather than empirically proven approach.

Activity 3 (50s/100s money and boundary work) has sourceClaims set to [] because none of the cited claims directly supports its money-anchoring/boundary-roll teaching principle; it is a research-informed proposal only.

The original research rated a 3D environment as adding 'no conceptual gain' for these planar patterns. That is a catalog fit judgement, not a pedagogical law; flat aligned views are proposed because the doubling overlay and hundred-square pattern read clearly in 2D, without claiming 3D cannot teach it.

The original keyRepresentation referred to a 'hundred square' for 50s/100s; a 1–100 square cannot show these to 1000, so a number line/track is used instead for those counts. The 4s/8s remain on the hundred square.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 8–9 (UK Y4, US Grade 3–4). Counting in 6s, 7s, 9s, 25s and 1,000s — the harder skip counts that complete the times-table set and extend into thousands.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y4 'count in multiples of 6, 7, 9, 25 and 1,000', 'find 1,000 more or less than a given number', and 'count backwards through 0 to include negative numbers'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 3.OA.7 fluent recall of products (the 6s, 7s, 9s underpin those tables); 4.OA.5 generate and analyse number/shape patterns; 4.NBT reading/place value into the thousands.
• Operational details: exploit structure so these are not brute memorised — 6s = doubled 3s; 9s carry a strong pattern (tens digit +1 while ones digit −1 each step, digit sum always 9, a clean diagonal on the hundred square); 7s have the WEAKEST pattern so need the most rehearsal, best built from 5s+2s; 25s are quarters/money/quarter-hours (four 25s = 100); 1,000s extend the place-value step and pair with backward counting through 0 into negatives.
• Checkpoint: skip-count and use structure to self-repair. Tier A (8): count in 6s and 25s from 0 and count in 1,000s. Tier B (8–9): count in 6s, 7s, 9s, 25s, 1,000s from 0 and find 1,000 more/less. Tier C (9): explain 6s as doubled 3s and use the 9s digit pattern (digit sum 9) to check a count, and count in 1,000s backwards through 0 into negatives.
bestPractices: Lead with structure, not brute rote: teach 6s as doubled 3s, and surface the 9s pattern explicitly (each step the tens digit rises by one and the ones digit falls by one, so the digits always sum to 9) so children have a self-check when a count wobbles.

Give the 7s the most rehearsal because they carry the weakest visible pattern — build them from known 5s and 2s (7 = 5 + 2) and from the array, and interleave them with already-secure counts rather than drilling in isolation.
Anchor 25s in quarters and money — four 25s make 100, 25p pieces, quarter-hours — so 25, 50, 75, 100 is felt as building whole hundreds from quarters rather than a memorised list.
Connect every count to its times table and to equal groups/arrays so counting in 6s, 7s and 9s is the fluency route into the ×6, ×7 and ×9 facts, not a parallel skill.

Teach 1,000s alongside 1,000-more/less and backward counting through 0 into negatives, using a number line that extends past 0 so the place-value step and the negative extension are seen on one continuous track.
keyRepresentations: Hundred square with the 9s shaded to reveal the diagonal and the digit-sum-9 pattern (and 6s to show doubled 3s)
Aligned number lines pairing 3s with 6s (doubling) and 5s+2s composing 7s
Equal groups / arrays for 6, 7, 9 linking each count to its multiplication table
Money and clock models for 25s (four quarters = 100, quarter-hours) and an extended number line through 0 for 1,000s and negatives
commonMisconceptions: Counting in 7s (and 6s/9s) as pure rote with no structural anchor, so a single slip cannot be repaired and the count derails.
Missing the 9s pattern and treating each step as '+10 then −1' incorrectly, e.g. writing 9, 18, 27, 37 by adding 10 and forgetting the −1.
Confusing adjacent tables (drifting between 6s and 8s, or 7s and 9s) because the steps feel similar and no pattern flags the error.
Mishandling 25s past 100 (25, 50, 75, 100, 125 becoming …100, 105) by reverting to a smaller or rounder step at the hundred.
Counting in 1,000s but stalling or reversing sign incorrectly when crossing 0 into negatives (…1000, 0, then '1000' again instead of −1000).

For9,18,…,90 the digits sum to9 and the tens-up/ones-down pattern is visible; it does not extend unchanged to99, whose digits sum to18. Use patterns as checks within their stated range.

feedback: For a term in the9-through90 segment, check the tens and ones sum to9. Do not mark99 wrong because its sum is18:99 is also a multiple of9. Beyond that segment, verify the jump or multiplication fact rather than requiring digit sum exactly9.
A common slip is applying '+10' alone (9, 18, 27, 37); point out the missing −1 on the ones digit and that 37's digits sum to 10, not 9.
If the 7s stall, rebuild the next term from the previous one plus 5 plus 2, or derive 7×6 from 7×5+7 (= 35 + 7 = 42) rather than counting on in ones.
At the hundred boundary in 25s (75 → 100 → 125), check the step stayed 25 and did not shrink to a rounder jump such as +5.
When crossing 0 in the 1,000s count, note the sign flips once: ...2000, 1000, 0, −1000, −2000 — not 1000 again.

Show the9-through90 tens-up/ones-down pattern, then display99 with digit sum18 rather than keeping a false locked9 meter. The 9s times table shows a digit-sum-of-9 / tens-up-ones-down pattern used as a self-check; 6s are taught as doubled 3s; 7s carry the weakest pattern and need most rehearsal.
learnerActions: Pick a count (6s, 7s, 9s, 25s, or 1,000s) and step it one jump at a time, saying each multiple aloud.

Step0,9,18,…,90. From9 to90, treat9 as09 if comparing tens and ones: the tens digit rises by1, the ones falls by1, and the digit sum is9. Then inspect99: its digits sum to18, so the earlier pattern does not continue unchanged.
For the 6s, show each 6-jump as two 3-jumps (the jump 0→6 is 3+3, and the jump 6→12 is a further 3+3), so each multiple of 6 is reached by pairs of 3-jumps.
For the 7s, build each step as a 5-jump plus a 2-jump (7 = 5 + 2) and rebuild any forgotten term that way.
For25s, partition a100-unit bar or collection into four equal25-unit parts, then continue25,50,75,100,125,150. A quarter-hour clock uses15-minute steps to60, so do not use it to label25-unit steps.
For the 1,000s, step along a number line that continues through 0 into negatives, and find 1,000 more or 1,000 less of a given number.

activities.title: Oral rehearsal partner for the weak 7s

activities.rationale: Spoken turn-taking rehearses the weakest-pattern 7s and prompts structural self-checks aloud. Because the key insight here is visual and structural, oral rehearsal supplements the generative pattern work; it is an oral-rehearsal affordance, not evidence that talk teaches the procedure better than other media.

When a 7s term is uncertain, check it by adding 7 to the previous term or by linking it to the matching ×7 fact (e.g. 7×4 = 28). The digit-sum-9 check belongs to the 9s count, not the 7s: 7s terms such as 14 or 28 do not have digit sum 9.

constraints: Use number structure: pair3-jumps for6, compose5+2 for7, partition100 into four25-unit parts, and continue1,000-unit steps through zero. Scope the9s tens-up/ones-down and digit-sum9 pattern to9 through90;99 has digit sum18.
Give the 7s the most rehearsal because they carry the weakest visible pattern; interleave them with already-secure counts rather than drilling in isolation.
Connect every count to its times table and to equal groups/arrays so counting in 6s, 7s and 9s is the fluency route into ×6, ×7 and ×9, not a parallel skill.

A fixed/reference hundred square can reveal and confirm patterns but cannot let the learner generate the count or watch the digit pattern update step by step; use it as a reference, not the sole teaching vehicle.
Short check questions verify counts and table links but do not by themselves build the pattern insight; pair them with activities where the learner generates the count.
Do not respond to sub-counting by ones with more chanting alone; build fluency through retrieval — derive from known facts, use number-line jumps, and keep practice short and daily.
For the 1,000s crossing 0, the sign flips exactly once (…1000, 0, −1000, −2000); avoid repeating a positive term after 0.

The digit-sum9 check used here applies to9 through90, with9 written as09 for a tens/ones comparison. It does not apply unchanged to99; do not reject a correct multiple of9 just because its digits sum to18.

topic.description: Count forwards and backwards in steps of powers of 10 (10, 100, 1000, 10,000, 100,000) for any given number up to 1,000,000

topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} count forwards and backwards in steps of 1,000 or 10,000 from any starting number — like 34,500, 44,500, 54,500 — without losing track?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 9-10. Count forwards and backwards in steps of powers of 10 (10; 100; 1,000; 10,000; 100,000) from any number up to 1,000,000 — e.g. count on in 10,000s from 462,000; back in 100,000s from 800,000. Each step changes ONE place, generalising the '10/100/1000 more' work to any power-of-ten step, with roll-over across boundaries.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Year 5): 'count forwards or backwards in steps of powers of 10 for any given number up to 1,000,000'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): builds on 4.NBT.1 place-value structure and skip-counting foundations.
• Operational details — Use a place-value chart / Gattegno chart and a number line: choose a step (which power of 10), and each count changes just that column — until a boundary forces a carry into the next column (e.g. counting in 10,000s past 990,000). Vary the step size and direction; predict the next terms of a sequence. Emphasise which digit ticks and when the roll-over cascades.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 9, emerging): counts on/back in a single power of 10 with no boundary. Tier B (age 9-10, secure): counts in any power of 10 to 1,000,000, naming the changing digit. Tier C (age 10, extending): handles roll-over boundaries and continues/predicts mixed sequences.
bestPractices: Name the step as a power of 10 and track which single column ticks each count.
Use a Gattegno chart / number line so the count is seen as one column changing (or cascading at a boundary).
Vary step size and direction (forwards/backwards) and cross boundaries deliberately.
Have children predict the next terms and articulate the rule.
Connect to the ×10 place-value relationship so the steps are structural, not memorised.
keyRepresentations: Gattegno / place-value chart (step ticks one column)
0-1,000,000 number line with power-of-ten hops
Sequence strips (predict next terms)
Place-value counters (add/remove one 10,000 etc.)
Digit-stepper display showing the changing digit
commonMisconceptions: Changing the wrong column for the chosen step.
Boundary errors when a column rolls over (990,000 + 10,000).
Losing track of direction (counting back but incrementing).
Reverting to counting in ones for large steps.
Not generalising the pattern across different powers of 10.

learn.summary: For ages 9-10: count forwards and backwards in steps of powers of 10 (10; 100; 1,000; 10,000; 100,000) from any starting number up to 1,000,000, generalising earlier '10/100/1,000 more' work. The core insight is that each step changes exactly ONE place-value column — until a column fills and a roll-over (carry) cascades into the next column. Learners choose a step size and direction, track which digit ticks, and handle boundary crossings such as counting in 10,000s past 990,000 (reaching 1,000,000) or 492,000 up to 502,000. Work spans emerging (single power of 10, no boundary), secure (any power of 10 to 1,000,000, naming the changing digit), and extending (roll-over boundaries and predicting mixed sequences).

activities.title: Single-column counting on a place-value chart
feedback: If the wrong column changes (e.g. 462,000 → 463,000 or → 562,000), point to the ten-thousands column on the chart and count again with only that digit moving; check the step size stays a constant ten-thousand each time.
If a learner reverts to counting in ones, re-name the step aloud ('I am adding ten-thousand, so the ten-thousands digit is what changes') and add one whole counter to that column.
If direction is lost (counting back but the digit increases), restate the direction before each step and confirm the number is getting smaller.
activities.rationale: Naming the step as a power of ten and tracking which single column ticks makes the count structural rather than memorised, and connects to the ×10 place-value relationship where each place is ten times the next. A place-value/Gattegno chart or counters let the one-column change be seen and physically enacted.
sourceClaims: Year 5 pupils should 'count forwards or backwards in steps of powers of 10 for any given number up to 1,000,000'.
Place-value structure (each place ten times the next) underlies counting in powers of ten (4.NBT.1).
Counting in powers of ten changes one place at a time with boundary roll-overs, best shown on a Gattegno chart/number line.
learnerActions: Choose a step that is a power of ten (10; 100; 1,000; 10,000; or 100,000) and a direction (forwards or backwards).
Starting from a given number such as 462,000, count on in 10,000s aloud: 462,000 → 472,000 → 482,000 → 492,000, each time saying which single column changed.
On a place-value chart (e.g. a Gattegno chart) or with place-value counters, add or remove ONE counter in the chosen column per step and read the whole number.

Say the count structurally too, keeping the unchanged places fixed: '46 ten-thousands and 2 thousand, 47 ten-thousands and 2 thousand, 48 ten-thousands and 2 thousand...' so only the ten-thousands count ticks while the 2,000 stays put.
Repeat for a different power of ten (e.g. count back in 100,000s from 800,000: 700,000 → 600,000 → 500,000) and name the column that now ticks.
activities.intendedInsight: Counting in a power of ten means repeatedly nudging a SINGLE place-value column up or down while every other digit stays frozen, as long as no boundary is crossed; the chosen step decides which column ticks. (When a column rolls over, e.g. 492,000 → 502,000, a neighbouring column changes too. This is covered in the boundary activity.)

activities.title: Crossing the boundary: the roll-over cascade
feedback: If 492,000 + 10,000 is given as 4,102,000 or the learner stalls, rehearse just the crossing: there are ten ten-thousands in one hundred-thousand, so the ten-thousands digit rolls from 9 back to 0 and the hundred-thousands increases by one, giving 502,000. Do not reteach the whole count — only rehearse boundaries.

If counting back stalls at a boundary (e.g. counting back in 10,000s from 502,000), pause at the crossing and ask which column must drop: the hundred-thousands digit decreases by one and the ten-thousands digit rolls back from 0 to 9, giving 492,000.

If the carry is applied to the wrong column, re-run the step slowly on the chart so each roll-over and carry is seen one column at a time (one carry for 492,000 → 502,000; two cascading carries for 990,000 → 1,000,000).
activities.rationale: Boundary roll-overs are the most common failure point and the place where the structure is most visible; isolating and rehearsing the crossing targets the error directly while keeping the single-column rule intact. A number line of equal power-of-ten hops and a chart showing the cascading carry make the mechanism concrete.
sourceClaims: Counting in powers of ten changes one place at a time with boundary roll-overs, best shown on a Gattegno chart/number line.
Year 5 pupils should 'count forwards or backwards in steps of powers of 10 for any given number up to 1,000,000'.
learnerActions: Count on in 10,000s and deliberately approach a boundary: 472,000 → 482,000 → 492,000 → 502,000, pausing at the crossing.
At 492,000, answer 'how many ten-thousands make the next hundred-thousand?' before stepping, then bridge to 502,000 and read the new hundred-thousands digit.
Count on in 10,000s up from 990,000 and watch the ten-thousands roll 9→0 while a carry cascades into the hundred-thousands and then the millions, reaching 1,000,000.

Count back in 10,000s across a boundary (522,000 → 512,000 → 502,000 → 492,000 → 482,000), noticing that at 502,000 → 492,000 the ten-thousands digit rolls back from 0 to 9 and the hundred-thousands digit decreases by one.
Predict a crossing before taking the step, then check: does only the next column change, or does the carry cascade further?
activities.intendedInsight: When a column fills, the single-column rule does not break — it cascades: counting forwards, the full column rolls over (9→0) and a carry moves into the next column, sometimes through several columns up to 1,000,000; counting backwards, an empty column rolls back (0→9) and the next column decreases by one.

activities.title: Spot the step and predict the next terms
feedback: If the step is misread, line up corresponding digits of two terms and ask which single column changed and by how much.
If next terms break the step size, restate the step and check each new term changes only the named column (unless a boundary forces a cascade).
For 375,000; 475,000; 575,000, confirm the step is +100,000 and the next term is 675,000; if a learner gives a non-constant step, compare each gap explicitly.
activities.rationale: Having children predict next terms and articulate the rule turns fluency into structural reasoning and lets secure learners meet boundary cases in a reasoning context. Continuing and predicting sequences cleanly works the generalised pattern of counting forwards and backwards in powers of ten.
sourceClaims: Year 5 pupils should 'count forwards or backwards in steps of powers of 10 for any given number up to 1,000,000'.
learnerActions: Look at an unlabelled sequence such as 375,000; 475,000; 575,000 and work out the step by comparing consecutive terms (here +100,000).
State the step as a power of ten and which column changes, then write or say the next three terms (675,000; 775,000; 875,000).
Try sequences that cross a boundary so a prediction requires a roll-over, e.g. continue counting on in 10,000s from 472,000 through 502,000.
Make and swap sequences with a partner: hide the upcoming terms and have them predict, then articulate the rule in words.
For a backwards sequence, confirm the terms decrease and name the changing column.
activities.intendedInsight: The counting pattern becomes reasoning: identifying a constant power-of-ten step lets you justify and predict any later term, including across boundaries.

constraints: Reading a count on a static annotated chart or choosing the next term from fixed options can serve as a reference or check, but recognition-only responses do not elicit the independent counting and roll-over handling that is the objective; learners should generate the counts themselves aloud, in writing, or by acting on a chart/counters.
Keep the step size constant within any one count; mixing step sizes mid-count is a separate, harder task and should be flagged, not assumed.
Always state the direction (forwards/backwards) explicitly so decreasing counts are not accidentally incremented.
Boundary crossings (e.g. 492,000 → 502,000; 990,000 → 1,000,000) are the key difficulty and must be practised deliberately, not left to chance.

Interactive examples (a step selector with one highlighted column that ticks, an animated carry cascade, a number-line toggle of equal power-of-ten hops, a hidden-term prediction mode) are optional ways to make the single-column mechanism concrete; they are helpful illustrations, not required equipment, and equivalent work can be done with a paper chart, counters, and spoken counting.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Of the cited sources, the DfE National Curriculum claim is marked verified; the CCSS 4.NBT.1 and NCETM Primary Mastery claims are marked unverified in the source row and should be checked before relying on them.

The original material framed dialogue and 3D models as poor fits and a static chart as merely 'possible'. These catalog-style rankings have been removed; a conversation can still support articulating the rule and a fixed chart can still teach as a reference, so no universal 'only an interactive can teach this' claim is asserted.
The legacy error example '492,000 + 10,000 = 4,102,000' is retained only as a learner MISCONCEPTION to diagnose and correct (correct answer 502,000); it is never presented as a valid result.

The structural reading '46 ten-thousands' for 462,000 is a UK-mastery shorthand that, taken literally, equals 460,000; the activity keeps the fixed 2,000 explicit so the whole number is read correctly while the ticking digit is highlighted.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Ages 5–6 (Year 1). COMPARING TWO WRITTEN NUMERALS 1–10 — deciding which of two symbols is greater or less (using 'greater than/less than', later >, <). The symbolic form of comparing quantities: the numeral must be reconnected to the amount it stands for.
• Standards — UK (DfE): NC Year 1 language 'equal to, more than, less than (fewer), most, least'; Year 2 introduces the <, >, = signs and 'compare and order numbers from 0 up to 100'. Single-digit numeral comparison is the Year 1→Year 2 bridge.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): K.CC.7 verbatim — 'Compare two numbers between 1 and 10 presented as written numerals' (built on K.CC.6, comparing groups by matching/counting).
• Operational details: Anchor each numeral to a QUANTITY (a set, a ten-frame, a number-line position) then compare — never a bare symbol trick. The NUMBER LINE is decisive: the numeral further RIGHT is greater. Introduce <, > as the mouth/arrow OPENING toward the larger number, but only AFTER meaning is secure (the 'alligator' mnemonic without meaning is a known trap). Distinguish the value of a numeral from its physical size on the page.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (5) given two single-digit numerals, says which is greater/less by linking each to a quantity or number-line spot. Tier B (5–6) compares reliably and reads/uses 'greater than / less than'. Tier C (6) places the correct >, < or = between two numerals and justifies by number-line position or matched quantities.
bestPractices: Reconnect numeral → quantity before comparing: show each numeral as a set / ten-frame / number-line point, so the comparison is of amounts, not squiggles.
Use the number line as arbiter — 'further right = greater'; this also settles equality and orders more than two numbers.
Introduce <, > meaningfully (the symbol opens toward the bigger number) and only after understanding — don't let the 'hungry alligator' mnemonic replace meaning.
Include equality: some pairs are equal, so comparison has three outcomes (>, <, =).
Separate value from appearance: a boldly printed '2' is not 'more than' a small '9'.

learn.summary: For ages 5–6 (Year 1 / Kindergarten), learners compare two written numerals from 1 to 10 and decide which is greater or less, using the words 'greater than / less than' and later the symbols >, <, =. The central idea is that a numeral stands for an amount: comparison must be grounded in quantity or number-line position, not in how the symbol looks on the page. The number line acts as the arbiter (further right = greater), and >, < are introduced as a sign that opens toward the larger number — introduced only after the quantity meaning is secure, and never reduced to a meaning-free 'hungry alligator' trick. Equality (=) is kept as a genuine third outcome.

activities.title: Anchor the numeral to its amount, then compare on a number line
feedback: If a learner draws dots or uses fingers for each numeral before deciding, treat this as the numeral-to-amount link still forming, NOT as a comparison error. Reinforce it by asking 'which is further along when you count?' and keep connecting each numeral to its number-line position; it bridges with practice.

If a learner picks by which digit looks bigger or is boldly printed, cover the printing and compare the two towers or ten-frames instead, showing that a boldly printed 2 is still fewer than a small 9.
To rehearse the 'smaller/less' direction, pair every comparison both ways on the number line ('7 is more than 4 AND 4 is less than 7') so both phrasings are practised together.
activities.rationale: Grounding each numeral in a set, ten-frame, or number-line point keeps the comparison about amounts rather than marks, and the number line gives a reliable rule that also handles ordering and equality.
sourceClaims: Comparing numbers is best anchored to quantity/number-line position; the < > symbols should be taught as opening toward the larger value, not by a meaning-free mnemonic.
learnerActions: Take two numeral cards, for example 4 and 7, and place each on a number line marked 1–10.
Beside each numeral build or reveal its quantity — a little tower of cubes, counters, or a filled ten-frame — so the amount behind the symbol is visible.
Say which is further along the line when you count, and therefore which is greater and which is less.
State the comparison out loud in BOTH directions: '7 is greater than 4 AND 4 is less than 7.'
Repeat with pairs that include an equal pair (for example 5 and 5) so you meet all three outcomes.
activities.intendedInsight: A written numeral names an amount; you compare the amounts, and the number line settles it because the numeral further right is greater. Equality is a possible result, so comparison has three outcomes (>, <, =).

activities.title: Place the >, < or = sign: > and < open toward the larger amount, = shows the amounts are the same
feedback: If a learner knows which number is bigger but writes the sign backwards (for example says '7 is bigger' aloud but writes 4 > 7), this is an orientation slip, not a magnitude error: have them read the written statement aloud, notice it says the wrong thing, and turn the sign so its open end faces the larger numeral.
Confirm a correct placement by pointing to the number-line gap: the sign opens toward the numeral that sits further right.
Avoid relying on a 'hungry alligator eats the bigger number' story alone — use it, if at all, only alongside the number-line meaning, because the mnemonic without meaning leads to backward signs.
activities.rationale: Introducing >, < as a sign that opens toward the larger value, after quantity meaning is secure, and checking by reading the statement aloud, directly addresses the common reversal error and the meaning-free mnemonic trap.
sourceClaims: Comparing numbers is best anchored to quantity/number-line position; the < > symbols should be taught as opening toward the larger value, not by a meaning-free mnemonic.
learnerActions: Keep the two numerals (with their towers/quantities visible) on the number line.
Choose and place the correct sign between them: >, <, or =.
Check the sign by its open end — the wide, open end should face the larger numeral/tower; the point faces the smaller.
Read the finished statement aloud exactly as written, for example '4 < 7' as 'four is less than seven'.
If what you read aloud does not match which number is actually bigger, flip the sign and read it again.
Try equal pairs so you also place the = sign.
activities.intendedInsight: The comparison sign is not a picture to memorise: when the amounts differ, the open end of > or < always faces the larger amount — the numeral further along the number line — and when they are the same, = is used. Reading the completed statement aloud is how you check it is correct.

activities.title: Compare and order from the numerals alone
feedback: Correct responses for the prompts above are 4 < 7, 9 > 6, 3 < 8, each read correctly, and 2 identified as smaller than 5.
If a learner must still draw dots or count fingers for each numeral before deciding, the magnitude link is still forming — return to the number line rather than marking it wrong.
If a learner reverses specifically on 'which is smaller / less', rehearse both directions together on the number line until both phrasings feel equally natural.
activities.rationale: Comparing with no objects present is what discriminates a secure written-numeral magnitude understanding from counting-dependent work, and justification by number-line position keeps the reasoning grounded.
sourceClaims: K.CC.7 verbatim: 'Compare two numbers between 1 and 10 presented as written numerals.'
Comparing numbers is best anchored to quantity/number-line position; the < > symbols should be taught as opening toward the larger value, not by a meaning-free mnemonic.
learnerActions: Given single-digit numeral pairs with no objects present — for example 4 __ 7, 9 __ 6, 3 __ 8 — decide for each which is greater or less and place the correct sign.
Read each completed comparison aloud ('four is less than seven', 'nine is greater than six', 'three is less than eight').
Answer 'which of 5 and 2 is smaller?' working directly from the numerals.
Put a short set of single-digit numerals in order from least to greatest.
Say how you know, using number-line position ('8 is further along when you count than 3').
activities.intendedInsight: Once the numeral-to-amount link is secure you can compare and order written numerals directly, without first building sets, and justify it by where each sits on the number line.

activities.title: Talk it through: who has more, and how do you know?
feedback: Prompt for justification, not just an answer: 'how do you know 7 is more than 4?'
If the learner forgets equality is possible, offer an equal pair and ask whether one must always be bigger.
activities.rationale: A short discussion can rehearse comparison language and reasoning; for this skill the written comparison is usually settled visually on the number line, so keep the talk linked to a number line or quantities to stay concrete.
sourceClaims: Comparing numbers is best anchored to quantity/number-line position; the < > symbols should be taught as opening toward the larger value, not by a meaning-free mnemonic.
learnerActions: Given two numerals or two small collections, say which represents more and explain your reasoning.
Use the words 'greater than', 'less than', and 'equal to' in your explanation.
Respond to follow-up questions such as 'which is further along when you count?' and 'could they ever be the same?'
activities.intendedInsight: Putting the comparison into words, including the possibility of equality, strengthens the link between the spoken comparison language and the written symbols.

constraints: Always anchor each numeral to a quantity (set, ten-frame, or number-line point) before comparing; never teach a bare-symbol trick.

Introduce >, < only after the quantity meaning is secure, and present them as a sign opening toward the larger number rather than as a meaning-free 'hungry alligator' mnemonic, which is a known trap that produces backward signs.
Always include equal pairs so learners experience three outcomes (>, <, =) and do not assume one number must be bigger.
Distinguish a numeral's value from its appearance on the page: a boldly or largely printed digit is not automatically greater.
A static number line with two numerals marked is a useful reference but does not let the learner test and place a sign themselves; use it as a scaffold, not the whole activity.

Recognition-only tasks (choosing from given options) can give useful practice but do not by themselves require the learner to orient and place the sign independently; include at least some tasks where the learner places or writes the sign.

A learner who still builds or counts sets for each numeral is at a developmental stage where the numeral-to-amount link is forming; this is a prerequisite still bridging, not a comparison error to be penalised — reconnect to the prerequisite on linking numerals to their magnitude (counting / number-line position).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit on examples: the stated comparisons are correct — 4 < 7, 9 > 6, 3 < 8, and 2 < 5. The sign-orientation rule (open end faces the larger number) and the number-line rule (further right = greater) are internally consistent.

Self-audit correction carried into the activities: the original wording leaned on the 'hungry alligator / mouth eats the bigger number' framing even while warning against it. The rewrite keeps the meaning-first rule ('open end faces the larger amount, checked by reading aloud') as primary and demotes the animal story to an optional aid only, because the source itself flags the meaning-free mnemonic as a trap that causes reversals.

For Activity 3, K.CC.7 is retained because 'presented as written numerals' maps closely to that activity's compare-from-numerals-alone principle.

Interactive-reveal details (towers growing from numerals, dragging a sign, a lit number-line gap) are retained as OPTIONAL illustrative mechanisms, not required technology.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 5–6 (LANGUAGE): read and write the number WORDS one–twenty, and connect each word to its numeral and quantity. This is the vocabulary/orthography layer over numerals 0–20.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y1): 'read and write numbers from 1 to 20 in numerals and words'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): supports K.CC/1.NBT number-name work; reading/writing number names in words is a Grade 1–2 literacy-of-number expectation aligned to 2.NBT.3 (read/write numbers using number names).
• Operational details — many number words are irregular sight words (one, two, eight) or phonically awkward, and the teens are doubly tricky: 'eleven'/'twelve' give no clue to ten-and-one, and 'thir-teen'/'fif-teen' hide their tens+ones structure and say the ones part first. The child decodes/blends the word, recognises irregular ones by sight, and maps word↔numeral↔quantity. Crosses into phonics (blending) and sight-word reading.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 5): read 'twelve' and identify it as 12; match numeral cards to word cards. Tier B (5–6): write the word form of a given number 1–20. Tier C (6): read and write all the words fluently including the irregular/teen forms, spelling them correctly.
bestPractices: Explicitly link WORD ↔ NUMERAL ↔ QUANTITY (three-way matching) so the word is read for meaning, not just decoded as text; builds on secured numerals 0–20 (prerequisite mt_fR0UtsSREU).
Treat irregular number words as SIGHT words (one, two, four, eight, twelve) taught alongside phonically decodable ones (six, ten) — coordinate with the phonics/high-frequency-word programme.

Give the teens special attention: 'eleven'/'twelve' are opaque and must be memorised; 'thirteen–nineteen' say the ones-word first (thir, four, fif...) then '-teen' — pair with a ten-frame to keep the ten-and-ones meaning attached.
Use number-word washing lines, labels around the room, and books/rhymes so the words are met in reading and writing repeatedly, not just in a maths drill.
Practise both directions — read a word to make/point to the quantity, AND write the word for a given numeral — to prevent word-recognition without production (or vice versa).
keyRepresentations: Triple-match cards: numeral (13) ↔ word (thirteen) ↔ ten-frame/quantity.
Number-word washing line 0–20 above the numeral track for constant reference.
Colour/segment cues on teen words (thir·teen, four·teen) highlighting the ones-part + '-teen'.
Word-and-numeral labelling of classroom objects and calendar for incidental exposure.
commonMisconceptions: Reading a number word as text without linking it to a quantity or numeral.
Spelling confusions: four/for, eight, nine→'nighn', and the many silent/irregular letters.
Teen/decade word muddles by sound: 'thirteen' vs 'thirty', 'fifteen' vs 'fifty'.
Assuming all number words are phonically regular and mis-decoding the irregular ones (one, two, eight).
Reversing the teen meaning because the word says the ones first (thir-teen → thinking 3 then 1 → 31).

learn.summary: For ages 5–6, learners read and write the number words one–twenty and connect each word to its numeral and its quantity (a three-way word↔numeral↔quantity mapping with a spelling/production component). Many number words are irregular sight words (one, two, eight, twelve). Some teen words are opaque ('eleven' and 'twelve' give no clue to ten-and-one or ten-and-two), and others say the ones-part first ('thir-teen', 'fif-teen'), so teaching should keep the ten-and-ones meaning attached while building sight-word recognition and correct spelling. Practise both reading (word→quantity) and writing (numeral→word) directions. A wider 0–20 reference range (washing line, chart) can support this, while the production target is the words one–twenty.

activities.title: Word–numeral–quantity triple match
feedback: If a learner says or writes 31 for 'thirteen' (31 is not one of the 0–20 cards), compare the quantities directly: building 31 would need three full tens and one more, whereas thirteen is one ten and three ones. Seeing the quantities can help the learner notice that 31 is far too big and correct the mistake.
When a match is correct, restate the three-way link aloud: 'thirteen — that's the numeral 13 and this many: ten and three.'
For the opaque words 'eleven' and 'twelve', confirm by sight and set out the matching quantity rather than expecting the word to sound out.
activities.rationale: Linking word↔numeral↔quantity and structure-linked sight-word teaching build reading for meaning on top of secured numerals 0–20, and acting on the quantity can help a learner notice and correct an error in an opaque or reversed teen word. A linked quantity frame makes the ten-and-ones structure visible; dragging onto numeral and frame are optional ways to make the mapping concrete.
sourceClaims: Many number words are irregular sight words and the teens are opaque (eleven/twelve) or say the ones-part first, so they need dedicated sight-word and structure-linked teaching.
learnerActions: Hear or read a number word such as 'thirteen'.
Place or drag that word card onto its numeral (13).
Place it onto a ten-frame or set showing one full ten plus three.
Match across the number words one–twenty (with 0–20 available as reference), including a playful pairs/memory game over the words.
Also work the reverse direction: given a numeral or a quantity, find and say the matching word.
activities.intendedInsight: The number word carries meaning: it names a specific numeral AND a specific quantity, so the word must be read for meaning, not just decoded as text.

activities.title: Build-the-word: spell the number for a numeral
feedback: Flag the four/for and 'thirteen'/'thirty' traps as they happen, contrasting the two spellings with their quantities.

If a young learner spells phonetically (e.g. 'fiveteen', 'elevin', 'nighn' for nine), treat it as normal early spelling: keep showing the correct written form and let spelling mature rather than marking it as a maths failure.
Praise correct production of irregular forms specifically, since these cannot be sounded out.
activities.rationale: Practising the writing/production direction prevents word-recognition without spelling (or vice versa), which the objective to read AND write the words requires. Treating phonetic invented spellings as developmentally normal avoids penalising expected early-years errors while still exposing correct forms.

activities.title: Teen zone: keep ten-and-ones visible
feedback: If a learner reads 'thirteen' as 31, re-point to the full ten plus three ones: the word means one ten and three, not three tens and one.
Contrast minimal pairs by sound and quantity: 'thirteen' vs 'thirty', 'fifteen' vs 'fifty', matching each to counters.

activities.rationale: Showing the ones-part + '-teen' beside a ten-frame for thirteen to nineteen, and pairing the opaque words eleven and twelve with their ten-and-ones frames, helps keep the ten-and-ones meaning attached to the teen words, directly targeting the known reversal and sound-alike confusions. Segment cues and the linked frame are concrete ways to show structure, not the only possible format.
sourceClaims: Many number words are irregular sight words and the teens are opaque (eleven/twelve) or say the ones-part first, so they need dedicated sight-word and structure-linked teaching.
learnerActions: Segment each teen word from thirteen to nineteen beside its quantity: thir·teen, four·teen, fif·teen, and so on.
Place each segmented word next to a ten-frame showing one full ten plus the ones part.
Memorise 'eleven' and 'twelve' as sight words paired with their ten-and-ones frames.
Say the word slowly and match it to the quantity, noticing that the ones-word comes first (thir-) but the quantity is ten-and-three.
activities.intendedInsight: The teens name ten-and-ones even though the word is opaque ('eleven'/'twelve') or says the ones-part first; keeping the structure visible helps prevent the reversal 'thir-teen → 31'.

activities.title: Number words in real reading and writing
feedback: If the wrong quantity appears after reading a word (e.g. 20 or 2 counters for 'twelve'), reteach the irregular word as a sight word alongside its numeral.
If a learner reads or writes the wrong member of a minimal pair (twelve/twenty), place the two words side by side with their quantities and say each slowly.
Confirm success when the learner acts on the word correctly and produces the word form, not merely when they recite a sequence.
activities.rationale: Encountering number words in authentic reading and writing (labels, lists, rhymes, washing lines) gives repeated meaningful exposure, and acting on a written word can expose genuine decoding of irregular words in context rather than recitation.

Read a word to make or point to the quantity, and write the word for a given numeral.
activities.intendedInsight: Number words are used to act in the world: reading one to do something and producing a word label shows real command beyond reciting.

activities.title: Reference wall: tap-to-hear number words 0–20
feedback: Encourage using the wall to self-check a spelling or a minimal-pair confusion rather than guessing.
Point out the highlighted ones-part + '-teen' when a word from thirteen to nineteen is in doubt; for eleven and twelve, point to the matching ten-and-ones quantity instead.
activities.rationale: A static numeral–word–quantity chart with optional tap-to-hear audio is a strong always-available reference for the words; however it supports recognition and recall and does not by itself have the child write/spell the words, which is half the objective, so pair it with production practice.
learnerActions: Use a 0–20 chart showing each numeral, its word, and a matching quantity.
Tap an entry to hear the word spoken and see the teen structure highlighted.
Return to the wall to check spelling and meaning while reading or writing elsewhere.
activities.intendedInsight: A consistent reference linking numeral, word and quantity supports recall of sight words and teen structure during other tasks.

constraints: Reading/recognition and matching tasks support consolidation but do not by themselves elicit independent spelling; include writing/production of the words to cover the full objective.
A reference chart or tap-to-hear wall supports recall but does not have the learner construct or spell the words; it is a scaffold, not the whole objective.
Build on secured numerals 0–20 as a prerequisite before layering the word forms.

Coordinate irregular number words (one, two, four, eight, twelve) with the phonics/high-frequency sight-word programme; do not assume all number words are phonically regular, and note that some (six, ten) are decodable.
Phonetic/invented spellings (fiveteen, elevin, nighn) in early writers are developmentally normal and should not be marked as maths failures; keep exposing correct forms as spelling matures.
Practise both directions (word→quantity and numeral→word) so recognition does not develop without production or vice versa.
The read/write production target is the words one–twenty; a wider 0–20 range may appear on reference displays as context.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Write any number 0–100 as a numeral from dictation
topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} read and write any number up to 100 — both as a numeral and by saying what it means?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 5–6: read and write NUMERALS 0–100 — extending secure 0–20 numeral reading/writing across the full two-digit range, leaning on the regular tens-and-ones pattern of the written system.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y1): 'count, read and write numbers to 100 in numerals'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 1.NBT.1 'count to 120 ... read and write numerals'; the numeral system to 100 is embedded here and in K.CC.3.
• Operational details — once 0–20 numerals and rote counting to 100 are secure, reading/writing to 100 is mostly about the REGULAR two-digit pattern: the left digit says the tens, the right digit the ones, and decade words map to the tens digit. The persistent trouble spots are the teens/twenties boundary and the said-first-heard-first mismatch (writing 'forty-two' as 24). This is procedural fluency, not yet full place-value reasoning (that is the two-digit-composition topic).
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 5): read two-digit numerals up to 100 on sight. Tier B (5–6): write any number 0–100 as a numeral from dictation. Tier C (6): read and write across a decade boundary (e.g. 79–80) and place/find numerals on a 0–100 grid without error.
bestPractices: Lean on the REGULAR pattern of two-digit numerals with a 100-square / Gattegno chart: the tens digit changes down the columns, the ones digit across the rows, making 0–100 a system rather than 100 things to memorise.

Directly rehearse the hear-it/write-it order for two-digit numbers where speech and writing agree in English above twenty (forty-TWO → 4 then 2) but the teens don't (thirteen) — contrast the two explicitly.
Practise decade boundaries (29→30, 79→80) which is where reading/writing and rote counting most often break down.
Keep numerals connected to quantity/position via a bead string or 0–100 number line so a two-digit numeral means 'this far along', not just two digits.
Give balanced read AND write practice (say-it → write it; show it → read it; point on the grid) to avoid one-way fluency.
keyRepresentations: 100-square and Gattegno tens-and-ones chart exposing the regular two-digit pattern.
0–100 bead string / number line linking each numeral to a position/quantity.
Place-value / arrow (Dienes) cards building 42 as 40 and 2 to reinforce which digit is which.
Decade-boundary number tracks (25–35, 75–85) for the tricky crossings.
commonMisconceptions: Transposing spoken two-digit numbers (writing 'forty-two' as 24) — confusing the ones-first teens with the tens-first pattern of the rest.
Decade-boundary errors when counting/writing (after 29 saying/writing 'twenty-ten', or 39→50).
Reading a two-digit numeral as two separate digits ('four, two' for 42) rather than as forty-two.
Miswriting the 'ty' decades (writing 70 as 17, confusing seventy/seventeen).
Omitting or misplacing 0 in decade numbers (writing 40 as 4, or 'forty' as 400).

learn.summary: For children aged 5–6 extending secure 0–20 numeral reading/writing to the full 0–100 range. The goal is procedural fluency in reading and writing two-digit numerals by exploiting the regular pattern (left digit = tens, right digit = ones), targeting the persistent trouble spots: the spoken-order transposition (writing 'forty-two' as 24), decade-boundary crossings (29→30, 79→80), and keeping the 0 in decade numbers. This is numeral fluency, not yet full place-value reasoning.

activities.title: Hear-it, build-it, place-it on a hundred square
feedback: If a learner writes 24 for 'forty-two', place both 24 and 42 on the grid and show how far apart they sit — the transposed numeral is visibly in the wrong region.

If a learner drops the zero when writing a decade number (writing 40 as 4, or 'forty' as 400), point out that the 0 holds the ones place so forty needs both digits and no extra ones; contrast 4 and 40 on the number line to show they are different sizes.
When a number is placed on the grid, an optional response is to light up the cell so a correct answer settles into the right column/row and a wrong one shows the mismatch in position.
For decade-boundary slips (saying 'twenty-ten' after 29, or 39→50), slow down and count along a bead string or number line so 29→30 is felt as one step forward.
Reinforce by linking the numeral to quantity/position on a bead string or number line so the written symbol stays tied to 'how far along'.
activities.rationale: Letting children act on the regular two-digit system — composing from tens and ones, writing from dictation, and seeing position feedback — is intended to build the pattern actively and to target the transposition, zero-omission and decade-boundary errors. Linking numerals to position/quantity keeps the symbol meaningful. Efficacy is proposed, not established.
sourceClaims: Year 1 pupils count, read and write numbers to 100 in numerals.
A 100-square / Gattegno chart exposes the regular tens-and-ones structure of two-digit numerals; decade boundaries and spoken-order transposition are the key difficulties.
learnerActions: Listen to a spoken two-digit number (e.g. 'sixty-eight') and write or point to its numeral.
Place the numeral in its position on a 100-square (state whether it is a 1–100 or a 0–99 layout), then check whether it lands where that number belongs.
Build a number from tens-and-ones cards: compose 42 by taking the '40' card and placing the '2' over its zero, so the tens and ones are explicitly separated.
Work across decade boundaries: continue 28, 29, __ and 78, 79, __ , writing each numeral (30 and 80).
Do both directions: say-it → write it; show it → read it aloud; point-to-it on the grid.
activities.intendedInsight: 0–100 is one regular system, not a hundred separate facts: moving down a column the tens digit goes up while the ones digit stays the same, and moving along a row the ones digit changes. On a 0–99 square each row shares one tens digit. On a 1–100 square the decade number (10, 20, … 100) ends each row, so it is the one cell in its row with a different tens digit. Either way, each numeral means 'this far along', not just two loose digits.

activities.title: Minimal-pair contrast: -teen versus -ty
feedback: If a learner writes 14 for 'forty', swaps 13/30, or confuses seventeen/seventy (writing 70 as 17), slow the word ending and contrast the pair with base-ten sticks (4 tens versus one ten and 4); firm the decade sequence by rote count.

If dictated teens come out reversed (41 for 'fourteen') while other numbers are fine, treat it as a normal transcription stage: keep modelling teens with a tens/ones frame and let exposure resolve it, rather than marking it wrong repeatedly.
activities.rationale: Minimal pairs isolate the genuine error types — auditory -teen/-ty confusion and teen transposition — so practice targets where fluency breaks rather than re-drilling secure numbers.
sourceClaims: A 100-square / Gattegno chart exposes the regular tens-and-ones structure of two-digit numerals; decade boundaries and spoken-order transposition are the key difficulties.
learnerActions: Read aloud the auditory -teen/-ty pairs: 13 and 30, 14 and 40, 17 and 70 (seventeen/seventy); then the separate reading-order/transposition pair 17 and 71 (seventeen/seventy-one).
Take dictation of 'forty' then 'fourteen'; write each and compare.
Explain or show how 40 and 14 differ, e.g. with base-ten sticks: forty is 4 tens; fourteen is one ten and 4.
Say the endings clearly: contrast the spoken ones-first teens (thir-TEEN) with the spoken tens-first rest (FORTY-two), while noting both are written tens-first (13 and 42).
activities.intendedInsight: The teens 13–19 are SAID with the ones idea first (a special '-teen' word), and eleven and twelve are irregular words. All of them, like every two-digit number, are WRITTEN tens-first (11, 12, 13, 14). Numbers from 20 up are both said and written tens-first. Seeing that teens are spoken in a different order from how they are written helps keep the two patterns apart and supports moving past writing 41 for fourteen as place value develops.

activities.title: Fluency check: read, write, place, order
feedback: A correct answer confirms fluency; a wrong one points back to the build/contrast activities — e.g. a transposition sends the learner to the tens-and-ones card build, a -teen/-ty slip to the minimal-pair contrast, a dropped zero back to placing 4 versus 40.
When a dictated 'forty-two' is written as 24, show the gap between 24 and 42 on the line rather than just marking it wrong.
activities.rationale: Two-digit numeral reading/writing is highly checkable in multiple formats; a check can consolidate and surface which specific trouble spot remains. It tests fluency rather than building the pattern insight, so it follows the active work; it does not by itself teach the pattern.
sourceClaims: Year 1 pupils count, read and write numbers to 100 in numerals.
learnerActions: Write the numeral for a spoken number (e.g. 'forty-two' → 42).
Read a shown numeral aloud (e.g. 68 as 'sixty-eight', not 'six, eight').
Place a numeral on a 0–100 line (e.g. position 68).
Order a short sequence across a decade boundary, e.g. fill the gaps around 29→30.
Write the number that is one more than 19 (20); write 'sixty-two' then 'twenty-six' and check they differ.
activities.intendedInsight: Reading and writing to 100 should be reliable in both directions and across decade crossings, with minimal pairs kept distinct and the zero kept in decade numbers.

constraints: Secure 0–20 numeral reading/writing and rote counting to 100 are prerequisites before extending to 100.

This is procedural numeral fluency, not full place-value reasoning (two-digit composition/decomposition is a separate topic); keep representations tied to quantity/position but do not assume full place-value understanding.
Writing teen numbers in spoken order (41 for 'fourteen') is a normal developmental transcription stage that matures with place value; do not drill it as a careless error or mark it wrong repeatedly.

A static tappable 100-square is a useful reference and can present a numeral and its word, but it cannot by itself rehearse the productive skills of writing from dictation or free reading; use it as a scaffold alongside writing/speaking practice.
Recognition-only (multiple-choice) responses confirm reading but do not elicit independent numeral writing; include actual writing-from-dictation for the production half of the skill.
Decade numbers keep the 0 as a ones-place holder (40, not 4 or 400); treat zero omission/misplacement as its own error alongside transposition and -teen/-ty confusion.

Teens are written tens-first (13, 14) just like all two-digit numerals; only the SPOKEN order of teens differs, so teach the spoken/written order distinction rather than implying teens are written ones-first.

Position-lighting, grid cells, card-dragging and spoken prompts are optional ways to make feedback concrete, not required mechanisms; the same work can be done on paper, with a bead string, or with spoken dictation.

Teens are only SPOKEN ones-first; they are written tens-first (13, 14) like every other two-digit numeral, which is precisely why writing 41 for fourteen is a mismatch error.
